title: Top media outlets fail to disclose who is bankrolling their AI reporters
summary: Major outlets like Time and The Verge aren't disclosing that their AI reporters are funded by a nonprofit backed by an Anthropic investor.
story: Matt Shumer, co-founder and CEO of OthersideAI, details Anthropic's new AI model, Mythos, on 'The Sunday Briefing'. The model's "emergent capabilities" to find software vulnerabilities autonomously raised alarms, prompting Anthropic to restrict public access. Shumer explains the proactive move of granting major companies and the US government early access to Mythos for cyber defense, anticipating future threats to critical infrastructure and national security.
Several major news organizations are hosting reporter fellows with salaries paid by donor-supported AI journalism groups—relationships that frequently go undisclosed.

The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism places fellows with outlets like Bloomberg, Time, NBC News, the Guardian and the Los Angeles Times. And while some outlets are alerting readers to those funding relationships, others aren’t, raising questions about how disclosure standards are applied.
The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism pays its fellows between $60,000 and $80,000, and fellows with at least five years of experience can make between $90,000 and $110,000.
AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’
HalluSquatting becomes more dangerous when an AI agent can download files and run terminal commands without close supervision. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

"Tarbell is committed to supporting independent journalism that demystifies the debates around this technology, holds the companies and people building it to account and fosters the discourse necessary to chart a path that benefits society," the group states on its website.

Tarbell has sponsored at least 28 journalists covering topics like Anthropic, deepfakes, AI in geopolitics, misuse, the economy and misinformation. On its website, the group states that it does not set the direction of its reporters’ work.
"Our donors have no editorial control over the work of Tarbell, our fellows, or our grantees. Tarbell does not accept anonymous donations greater than $10,000," the website says.
The group also emphasized the policy in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"All our fellows maintain strict editorial independence. Tarbell does not dictate the conclusions or perspectives of the journalists we support — their reporting is guided only by facts they uncover, not predetermined narratives. This is outlined in our editorial independence policies, which are strongly emphasized throughout the process of recruiting, vetting, and training the fellows," Cillian Crosson, executive director of the Tarbell Center, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Even so, Tarbell says it receives funding from Coefficient Giving, the Future of Life Institute, the EA Infrastructure Fund and the Survival and Flourishing Fund — all groups that advocate for their ideals on AI safety. Coefficient Giving in particular has awarded more than $4.7 million to Tarbell, according to the organization's public grants database.
More pointedly still, Coefficient Giving is backed primarily by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, an Anthropic investor.
In the case of Anthropic, many of Tarbell’s fellows have written material covering the company.

Harry Booth, a reporter working with TIME, wrote an article titled "The War for AI," calling Claude, Anthropic’s flagship AI, a "world-class model" after visiting the company’s California headquarters. TIME did not disclose Booth’s support from Tarbell in his story.
ABC NEWS FACES BACKLASH FOR PRESENTING OBAMA CAMPAIGN AD AS AN 'EXCLUSIVE' ON REDISTRICTING MEASURE

In this photo illustration, the American weekly news magazine and news website Time logo seen displayed on a smartphone with an Artificial intelligence (AI) chip and symbol in the background. (Budrul Chukrut/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Similarly, The Verge did not mention reporter Robert Hart’s paid fellowship as he authored an article on OpenAI, the parent company of ChatGPT, when he covered the Trump administration’s clash with Anthropic over security concerns.
TIME said disclosure decisions are left to its editors.

"TIME is committed to transparency. Current Tarbell Fellows’ affiliations are disclosed in their TIME author biographies. TIME’s editorial decisions are determined solely by our editors," the outlet said in a statement.
The Verge did not respond to requests for comment.

Notably, some outlets have chosen to outline connections to Tarbell at the bottom of their stories. NBC News added an editorial note to the work of Jared Perlo, a fellow who reports on the Future of Life Institute, a group that evaluates AI safety.

"This reporter is a Tarbell Fellow, funded through the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, a nonprofit devoted to supporting the news coverage of artificial intelligence," NBC wrote at the bottom of the report.
OPENAI'S SAM ALTMAN WANTS TO NEGOTIATE A 5% STAKE IN COMPANY FOR US IF COMPETITORS AGREE TO KEY PROVISION

University of Chicago leaders announced new AI-focused education policies, including a ban on electronic devices in first-year law classrooms and expanded instruction on the ethical use of artificial intelligence. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The Tarbell Center has received funding from the Future of Life Institute, which is a subject of this article. The Tarbell Center had no input on NBC News’ reporting," NBC added in their disclosure note.

Tarbell in a statement to Fox News Digital said that, for its part, it requires fellows and outlets to be transparent about their placement, funding and relationship with the organization. It noted that some fellows no longer are required to disclose those connections if and when they're hired by their host publication.

"Transparency is a core principle for Tarbell. As laid out in our policies, we require all fellows and placement outlets to disclose Tarbell’s support on the fellow’s author page. As we’re between fellowship cycles at the moment, we currently only have six Tarbell fellows who are actively reporting," Crosson said.

"All six fellows disclose their Tarbell support on their author page. Several recent Tarbell fellows have since been hired full-time by their publications: Since they’re no longer funded by Tarbell, they won’t have such a disclosure on their author pages."
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trade vessel struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz amid US-Iran talks
summary: A trade vessel reported being struck by an unknown projectile near Oman's coast as Trump claims a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is imminent.
story: President Donald Trump issues a stern warning to Iran, calling upcoming negotiations their 'last chance' to reach an agreement. Reporter Trey Yingst details the rising tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
A trade vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported being struck by a projectile overnight Tuesday as it was transiting near the coast of Oman.

The incident, reported to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations, comes amid conflicting reports of Iran participating in peace talks with the U.S. this week. President Donald Trump said on Monday that a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and denuclearize Iran was "imminent."

The UKMTO offered few details about the incident, saying only that the vessel had been struck "by an unknown projectile" at roughly 2 a.m. local time while it was 23 miles northeast of Al Khasab in Oman. The UKMTO did not clarify the name of the vessel or what flag it was flying under, nor did it note any injuries from the incident.
The British maritime security firm Ambrey confirmed the ship suffered damage but did not elaborate.
US CLAWS BACK KEY CONCESSION TO IRAN AFTER FRESH ATTACKS ON COMMERCIAL SHIPS IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
The incident comes as Iran has denied engaging in talks with the U.S., despite statement from multiple parties that talks are indeed ongoing.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday said all parties were engaged in mediation and are "looking into a diplomatic solution."
A spokesman for Iran's foreign ministry denied talks with the U.S. on Monday, saying Tehran was only involved in negotiations with Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz.
A navy vessel is seen sailing in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which much of the world's oil and gas passes on March 1, 2026. (Sahar AL ATTAR / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump acknowledged the mixed messages with frustration in a number of statements on Monday, insisting that Tehran officials were engaged in talks with the U.S. regardless of what they were saying publicly.
TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

"They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’ talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
A satellite image shows an oil slick next to the Caroline Bezengi, a sanctioned vessel off the coast of the Dhofar Governorate, Oman, July 28, 2026. (Planet Labs PBC/Handout via REUTERS)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For some reason they, when they're talking they don't like saying that they're talking," Trump said later during an Oval Office event. "So I say we're in talks, big deal, we're in talks. And they'll sometimes deny it even thought they spend hours and hours together talking."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Bad bosses on Capitol Hill could face reckoning under new anonymous staffer review platform
summary: Capitol CNCT lets verified congressional staffers anonymously rate and review their offices, revealing early rankings of the best and worst bosses.
story: Former congressional staffer David Tennent explains Capitol CNCT's "The Scoop," a new verified online platform he created so Capitol Hill employees can anonymously rate and review the offices they work in and the lawmakers who run them.

Capitol Hill staffers typically rely on private conversations and faceless social media accounts to identify toxic offices — but a new platform is offering a verified place to anonymously rate and review members of Congress and the workplaces they run.

Capitol CNCT, a program designed to centralize resources for congressional staffers, launched on July 20 a new tool called "The Scoop," where verified staffers can share anonymous, but verified, reviews of the offices where they're employed.

Former staffer David Tennent told Fox News Digital he founded Capitol CNCT to modernize the experience for young people working in congressional offices in Washington, D.C. He said the idea of the new ranking system emerged due to growing frustration over the number of 'bad bosses' and 'toxic offices' in the halls of Congress.
CAPITOL HILL SEX SCANDALS TRIGGER NEW PUSH TO REDRAW THE LINE FOR LAWMAKERS
The west front of the U.S. Capitol Building is reflected in the reflecting pool at dusk on July 22, 2026, in Washington, DC. (J. David Ake/Getty Images)

"I wanted to create something that gave a little bit more transparency to the process and help staffers find the best opportunities available," he said in an interview detailing his inspiration for the new tool.
Just a week after launch, verified reviews are already beginning to paint an early picture of workplace culture across Capitol Hill.

While most offices still have only a handful of ratings, the highest-rated House offices among them so far are Reps. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., Brendan Boyle, D-Penn., Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, and Robert Garcia, D-Calif.
Among Senate offices, the top five were Sens. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., Todd Young, R-Ind., Thom Tillis, R-N.C., Eric Schmitt, R-Miss., and Kevin Cramer, R-N.D.

Across both chambers, the five lowest-rated offices were Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo.
The offices of Davis, Krishnamoorthi, Brownley, Van Hollen and Bennet did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on their rankings.
ANGER SWELLS AFTER SWALWELL'S 'OPEN SECRET' WITH WOMEN WENT UNREPORTED FOR YEARS
There is no centralized human resources department for members’ offices on the Hill — making it tricky for staffers to report toxic or abusive workplaces.

"The Scoop" aims to offer a reliable place where people can leave and review feedback from staff who have gone through a verification process, which ensures anyone leaving a review actually works in the office they are rating.

"We verify the office in which they've worked," Tennent told Fox News Digital. "We sift through all reviews before they go live to our platform to make sure that staffer has actually worked in that office."
House lawmakers sit in the chamber on Capitol Hill. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Reviews are only published if the user leaving feedback passes Capitol CNCT’s background screening to ensure they have at some point worked for the member of Congress they are commenting on. The process includes verifying House and Senate email addresses attached to the account are legitimate.

"My biggest fear was just creating like a political retribution platform, right?" Tennent explained. "Where you can just go on and destroy people without any evidence or verification that you've been a part of that process."
Tennent revealed that Republican offices are almost twice as likely to be reviewed than Democrats’ offices so far.
The launch last month comes amid heightened scrutiny of workplace culture on Capitol Hill after multiple offices faced misconduct allegations this year.
REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER WELCOMES HOUSE ETHICS PROBE INTO SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS AGAINST HIM
Many members of Congress have either resigned or been under fire this year for allegations of inappropriate behavior with members of their staff.

Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, both resigned in April after staffers from their offices came forward with accusations of sexual misconduct — including rape accusations against Swalwell.
"We happened to be able to launch it right in this timeframe where this congressional ethics or lack of morality discussion is really hitting its high pitch," Tennent said.

Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-CA) speaks alongside Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI) during a news conference on the introduction of their Protection from Abusive Passengers Act at the U.S. Capitol Building on April 06, 2022 in Washington, DC. Swalwell and Reed's legislation is designed to improve air safety, increase traveler protections, reduce in-flight violence and hold unruly passengers accountable if they assault flight attendants and airline crew members. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Tennent said that while the main purpose of the app is to give staffers, or those considering working on the Hill, verifiable reviews about what it is like working for certain members of Congress, he also hopes it will serve as constructive criticism for members and their offices "to create a better working Congress."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We do want to provide like constructive criticism in this process," Tennent said

He continued, "Our hope is that if a chief of staff or a member sees that their office is very poorly rated, that over time they're gonna go, ‘Oh, this is a wake-up call for me. Let me implement some strategies to boost office morale, to change how we communicate with each other . ’"
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: WATCH: GOP senator unloads on 'creature of Washington' challenger in critical Senate showdown
summary: Jon Husted says Sherrod Brown's 32 years in Washington produced nothing but higher energy prices and liberal votes out of step with Ohio voters.
story: Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital Sherrod Brown's decades-long Washington record remains his biggest liability as the high-stakes Senate race heats up.

MARYSVILLE, OH - The Ohio Senate race could very well decide the balance of power in the U.S. Senate in November and incumbent Republican Jon Husted is making the case that the reasons his Democratic opponent was voted out of office two years ago are still relevant today.

"He’s spent 32 years in Washington, and he's got nothing to show for it, the voters over here in Ohio know it," Husted told Fox News Digital at the annual Summer Farm Fest on Sunday when asked about his race against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

"That's why they sent him packing two years ago. He was defeated by Bernie Moreno by over 200,000 votes. This is all he's done. He's been in an elected office since 1974. He hasn't done anything in the private sector. He's just been a creature of Washington and I think the voters finally are tired of it. That's why they sent him packing. I don't think they're gonna have any enthusiasm for rehiring him for a job that he failed at."

After representing Ohio in the Senate for almost two decades after years of serving in the House of Representatives, Brown was defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 in a blistering campaign that was one of the most expensive in U.S. history. Moreno consistently tied Brown to the unpopular positions of then-President Joe Biden, and Husted told Fox News Digital those concerns still exist, particularly on immigration.
FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS
Fox News Digital spoke to Republican Sen. Jon Husted about his race against challenger Sherrod Brown in a closely watched Senate campaign. (Fox News Digital/Getty)

"We had basically an invasion of 11 million people," Husted said. "He supported amnesty for them. He supported Social Security payments for illegals, healthcare for illegals, COVID checks for illegals. The sanctuary cities he supported led to crime, fentanyl, human trafficking in our state, and it's been terrible, and the voters know this."

"They know that he failed them. They know when he goes off to Washington with his comrades that he votes like a liberal, that he's too liberal for Ohio, that he has a track record of voting with Bernie Sanders and Kamala Harris and Joe Biden, and that's out of step with where Ohio is."

Over the last few weeks, Brown has blanketed the airwaves with ads criticizing Husted on data centers, a hot-button issue in Ohio, arguing that Husted’s support of data centers over the years has resulted in higher energy prices for consumers.
Husted, who was appointed to the Senate in January 2025 after the departure of now-Vice President JD Vance, pushed back on that assertion when asked about the ads.

"He had 32 years in Congress, he did nothing about it, and I, in my, just briefly over a year there, have legislation to require data centers to build their own power, to pay their own way, and to give the benefits of their presence to the citizens of those local communities, rather than the way that Sherrod Brown has done it, where he's failed," Husted explained.
DEM SENATE CANDIDATE SHERROD BROWN CLAIMS HE SUPPORTS 'CLOSING THE BORDER'; GOP SAYS RECORD PROVES OTHERWISE
Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat from Ohio, during a campaign event at the Steubenville City Building in Steubenville, Ohio, on Friday, Oct. 11, 2024. (Justin Merriman/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Husted continued, "This is the problem with the guy, is that he does nothing, and then a problem comes out, and he says, blame that person… He didn't do anything about it. He never does anything about it. He just waits for problems to happen. And then he says, well, it's the other person's fault. It's time to hold him accountable."
Husted made the case that the policies Brown supported in Congress led to the high energy rates the country is seeing now.

"He spent 32 years in Washington and didn't do anything except raise our electricity prices because he and the radical climate change agenda shut 23 power plants in Ohio," Husted said. "If we had those 23 power plants today, we wouldn't have high energy prices."
Husted continued, "Him voting for Obamacare, which has doubled the price of health care insurance in the state of Ohio and around the country. He needs to be held to account for his failed policies."

While Ohio has historically been known as a bellwether swing state, President Donald Trump won the state convincingly in 2016, 2020 and 2024, shifting the Buckeye State to a reliably red stronghold. However, recent polling, including a Fox News poll in June, shows Husted trailing Brown as Republicans battle the historical headwinds of the party in power struggling in midterm elections.

Brown, recruited back into politics in part by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, is looking to flip one of the four seats Democrats need to regain control of the Senate, with Ohio among the party's top pickup opportunities alongside Alaska, Maine and North Carolina.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Senator Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Feb. 13, 2025. (Getty Images)
With less than 100 days to go until the midterms, Husted says that Brown’s record will be front and center.

"Just showing the contrast between 32 years of failure from Sherrod Brown and the fact that I'm an Ohio guy, I've fought for Ohioans, I've helped in state government to turn this state in the right direction," Husted said. "We now have more jobs than we've ever had in our state's history, the lowest unemployment rate, frankly, than we ever had in our states' history. And we don't need to send this guy back to Washington, Sherrod Brown, to continue the failed policies that have harmed the country and harmed our state. We need a guy like me who will fight for Ohio."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Brown campaign for comment.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Historian blasts Smithsonian's activism shift after first visit in over a decade: 'Completely different place'
summary: Dr. Jody Edward Ginn says the Smithsonian National Museum of American History abandoned education for activism after visiting for the first time since 2012.
story: Dr. Jody Edward Ginn, historian and museum professional, told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from education to activism after his recent visit.

A historian and museum professional accused the Smithsonian of abandoning its educational mission in favor of activism following his visit to the National Museum of American History (NMAH) for the first time in more than a decade amid mounting criticism from the Trump administration and conservatives over how the museum presents American history.
"It's a completely different place than when I was there in 2012," Dr. Jody Edward Ginn told Fox News Digital.

"Its mission is clearly exactly what they changed it to be. It is a museum for activism. They use history, but that's kind of the problem. You know, scholars of history, and I don't consider these folks scholars anymore. They're activists."

After reading the administration's Domestic Policy Council report accusing the Smithsonian and the NMAH of failing to present history "in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic," Ginn said he traveled all the way from Texas to see it for himself.
INSIDE THE BEHEMOTH SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM NETWORK DRAWING FIRE FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

Dr. Jody Edward Ginn told Fox News Digital the Smithsonian has shifted from its educational mission toward activism after visiting the museum for the first time since 2012. (Fox News Digital ; Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
"From the moment I walked in, it's a very different experience," Ginn said. "Now, I wasn't totally shocked by this because I've been watching this evolution in my field for over a decade."
As he made his way through the exhibits, Ginn said the institution seeks to "specifically direct" visitors "to action" rather than give them the information to "make their own decisions."
"It became this goal, their own stated goal, to turn museums from institutions of education, of public education, into institutions to encourage activism, which could also be said to indoctrinate."
Ginn said he found "factually incorrect information" in some exhibits but argued what they don't tell visitors is just as misleading.
WATCH: SMITHSONIAN HISTORY MUSEUM DIRECTOR STUMBLES OVER BASIC QUESTIONS ON SEX: ‘I’M NOT SURE’

Anthea Hartig, director of the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History, testifies during the House Oversight and Government Reform Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past," in Rayburn building on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"The biggest problem is in what they leave out," he said.

Ginn argued the museum's "graphic" and sexually explicit exhibits have no place in a museum frequented by children and families, saying they're "out of sync with what museums were just a few years ago."
"These are geared towards all ages," he said. "Why would you do that? All of that's out of sync with what museums were just a few years ago."
In a House hearing last month, lawmakers raised similar concerns during a House hearing, pressing Smithsonian National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig about the museum's exhibits.

Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., asked Hartig about the exhibit titled "Illegal to Be You: Gay History Beyond Stonewall," which featured a bondage harness, saying "You have pictures of bondage, you have some overtly sexual things up there, you have transgender folks."

Lawmakers also questioned Hartig about the 2017 MASS Action Toolkit, a guide for museum professionals that references the 2014 Ferguson, Missouri, police shooting and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests while describing "objectivity" as a characteristic of "white supremacy culture," which Ginn said was part of its effort to lean towards activism.
SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT
The Smithsonian, the nation's largest museum and research complex, is at the center of a White House campaign to overhaul its presentation of American history. (J. David Ake/Getty Images)
Reflecting on the testimony, Ginn said it was "very disappointing" and did not represent "a scholarly presentation whatsoever."
"If that's the kind of museum you've been approved to run, then just own it," he said. "Don't say you're being unbiased when it's really evident."
Ginn also criticized Hartig for maintaining that the museum has not taken a side, adding its revised mission statement "changed the purpose of that museum."

During a 2024 presentation to undergraduate and graduate history students, Hartig explained the museum removed the mention of "American history" from its mission statement because it was "hard to get out of the 'America First' mentality."

For Ginn, his visit confirmed what he described as a "massive shift" in the museum profession, with the Smithsonian serving as "the highest-profile symptom of a process that's been going on for some time."

"It is my opinion as a public historian that the mission we've always had is to educate the public and provide scholarly information," he said. "To me, that's what the National Museum of American History should be."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
However, Ginn said he is "not hopeful" the institution can change without a "massive effort" to replace current staff with people he believes would prioritize history over politics.
"You're going to have to put in new people who are committed to scholarly standards and non-politicized educational programming," he said. "These people have bought into it, hook, line and sinker."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Smithsonian for comment.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: El-Sayed touts endorsement from pastor who praised notorious antisemite infamous for calling Jews ‘termites’
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's campaign paid $75,000 in consulting fees to a Detroit pastor who once praised Louis Farrakhan's leadership at a 2013 gathering.
story: Michigan Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed campaigns with left-wing influencer Hasan Piker despite his history of offensive comments on 9/11 and antisemitism. Piker, known for calling America deserving of 9/11 and showing no patriotism, has a significant online following. Some Democrats fear this controversial alliance could jeopardize their chances in the crucial Michigan Senate race during the midterms, alienating swing voters.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is enthusiastically touting the endorsement of Horace Sheffield III, an influential Detroit pastor and radio host who once heaped praise on Nation of Islam minister Louis Farrakhan.

Sheffield endorsed El-Sayed on air in November 2025, with the Senate hopeful issuing a press release to commemorate the occasion and saying that he was "deeply honored" to have his support. In May 2013, Sheffield gave a speech introducing Farrakhan to a gathering of religious leaders where he praised the controversial cleric for his leadership and accused outside forces of slandering him.
"We need someone to give us direction. I believe we have a leader here that can organize us," Sheffield said, referring to Farrakhan, according to a media outlet founded by Farrakhan.
Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, at a campaign event in Detroit, Michigan on August 2, 2026. ( )
MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS
Before Sheffield lauded the Nation of Islam leader, he had racked up an extensive record of controversial remarks slammed as anti-Semitic or as instances of anti-White racism.

In 1996, for instance, Farrakhan accused Jews of being "wicked deceivers of the American people" who have "sucked their blood." A year later, he suggested that "people will never be free in this country" until they are liberated from the "tremendous amount of influence" Jews exert over the American government.
Shortly before Sheffield praised Farrakhan in May 2013, the Nation of Islam minister stated that "Jews are the most violent of people" in February 2012.
WIFE OF LOUIS FARRAKHAN DEAD AT 90

Honorable Minister Louis Farrakhan, National Representative of The Honorable Elijah Muhammad and The Nation of Islam, speaks onstage during Nipsey Hussle's Celebration of Life at STAPLES Center on April 11, 2019, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images For All Money In Records and Atlantic Records)
Farrakhan also called White people "the skunk of the planet earth" and suggested that Europeans are not yet fully evolved human beings.
Following these controversial statements, Sheffield suggested during his 2013 introductory remarks that Farrakhan was a truth teller whom the establishment was trying to silence.
"They want to silence people who tell us the truth, and we know why this is happening and who is doing it, but we need some help with how to overcome it," Sheffield said during his speech.
ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK
Louis Farrakhan and Abdul El-Sayed. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images | Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
After the 2013 event, Farrakhan continued his habit of controversial remarks, calling Jews "termites" in 2018.
Despite Sheffield’s praise of a highly controversial cleric, El-Sayed’s campaign has worked with him to a considerable degree.

In June, Sheffield stopped by El-Sayed’s campaign office to record a promotional video for the candidate. More recently, the Washington Free Beacon reported that the El-Sayed campaign had paid a nonprofit run by Sheffield $75,000 for "consulting" fees between October 2025 and June of this year.

Sheffield’s previous radio station suspended him in 2018 after he endorsed Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar’s failed bid for Michigan governor after accepting tens of thousands of dollars in "consulting" fees from him, according to the Free Beacon.

While Sheffield’s controversial past associations could provide Republicans with ammunition to use against El-Sayed in the general election, especially given the accusations of antisemitism surrounding his campaign, the pastor's endorsement could also help him win the support of Black Michiganders, a demographic he has so far failed to impress.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I’m deeply honored to have Rev. Sheffield’s support. His lifelong commitment to justice, faith, and service embodies the very best of Detroit," El-Sayed said following the endorsement. "We’re building a coalition that believes politics should be about people, and together we’ll fight to deliver dignity, opportunity, and equity for every Michigander."
Representatives for El-Sayed and Sheffield did not return requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

title: GOP party fissures exposed in battle for SC Senate seat to replace Graham: 'I don't like hearing that'
summary: Five GOP candidates clashed over the filibuster, the Iran war and data centers in South Carolina's heated Senate debate to fill Lindsey Graham's seat.
story: Despite large agreement elsewhere, Darline Graham Nordone is prioritizing voter identification legislation. (Credit: WIS - Aug. 3)

The five GOP candidates that appeared in South Carolina’s U.S. Senate debate on Monday evening touched on several key issues of national importance as they made their case to fill the seat of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who died while in office last month.

Although candidates remained united on broad issues of party consensus, the debate exposed a fraying of opinion on topics like the war in Iran, U.S. government spending, the filibuster and data center expansion, highlighting the influence of even just one Senate seat.
The candidates include Sen. Darlene Graham Nordone, R-S.C., Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Rep. Russel Fry, R-S.C., businessman Mark Lynch and former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford.
REPUBLICANS DEFY TRUMP, JUMP INTO SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE HIS HANDPICKED SUCCESSOR

Senator Darline Graham Nordone, a Republican from South Carolina, at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Monday, July 20, 2026. Senate efforts to pass a landmark cryptocurrency bill hit a snag last week as Democratic negotiators indicated they don't yet support the latest GOP framework and some members balked at their narrowing window to act. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The biggest clash of the night came from Graham’s own sister, the appointee currently filling his seat.

Nordone, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement, announced she would vote to end the filibuster — a procedural hurdle that prevents the chamber from passing most legislation without 60 votes. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the chamber.

"And I am all for — this is where I differ from my brother — getting rid of the filibuster to get this done, because eventually the Democrats are going to get rid of it anyway," Nordone said, noting the major break with her late brother.

While supporters of the filibuster argue it prevents parties from strong-arming their views into law without bipartisan input, acting as one of the country's last bastions of moderation, the rule has throttled several Republican priorities called for by President Donald Trump, including national voter identification legislation.

Mark Sanford, another candidate who formerly served as governor of South Carolina, also touched on a topic of controversy on Monday by alluding that Congress — not the president’s discretion — should set the direction for the war in Iran.

"Only Congress has the authority to declare war. This decision needs to be made by Congress … body bags don't go back to Washington. They come back to home states and congressional districts," Sanford said.

It has been nearly six months since the U.S. originally bombed Iran in coordination with Israel, killing Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The conflict has stretched well beyond the timeline the administration said it had expected.
WAR POWERS RESOLUTION FAILS AS SENATE REPUBLICANS STAND BY TRUMP ON IRAN
Smoke rises over the city center after the Israeli army launches a second wave of airstrikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026. (Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images)

In the time since, debate among lawmakers has raged over whether the president has overstepped his authority and started a war — a power granted to Congress under the U.S. Constitution — and whether lawmakers should pass legislation to restrict his abilities.
Besides Sanford, other candidates seemed to support Trump, citing a concern over Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
One candidate, Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., qualified that support by affirming he would not support deploying U.S. service members to the area.

"No boots on the ground. I’m not a believer in that. My brother served in Iraq, and I’ve lost friends in foreign wars. But we can finish the mission by defanging Iran and making sure they have no capabilities left," Fry said.

In yet another area of division, Mark Lynch, a South Carolina businessman, raised the issue of data centers, a somewhat niche policy concern that’s rapidly raising questions of how national security interests are balanced against local interests and energy consumption.
While Republicans remain split on the issue, Lynch said he would favor prioritizing local community concerns.
"It is a pain point for South Carolinians," Lynch said, referring to the expansion of the centers.

"We're tired of waking up and seeing 100 acres of trees bulldozed, and we're told the data center is going to go right next to our neighborhood. It is horrible noise pollution. They're robbing our water. It takes millions of gallons to cool the data centers, and it's causing our electric utilities to increase. We already have a problem with inflation and affordability."
Although the debate remained largely restrained, Nordone needled Lynch in her closing remarks over several criticisms of her brother.
Lynch had criticized the late senator’s track record on amnesty and the legalization of marijuana.

"Mr. Lynch mentioned Lindsey Graham multiple times, and I don't know if he's just afraid Lindsey beat him, and now his little sister is going to beat him. But I just don't like hearing that," Nordone said.
Lynch ran against Linsey Graham in the 2026 primary earlier this year, before his death. Graham soundly defeated Lynch in a 56.8% to 28.9% win in June.
WATCH: DEMOCRATS ADMIT WHEN THEY'D ELIMINATE THE FILIBUSTER AS SAVE ACT FIGHT HEATS UP

U.S. Senator Darline Graham Nordone (R-SC), sister of the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC), mourns by his casket during a Congressional Tribute in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on July 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Nathan Howard-Pool/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lynch did not have an opportunity to respond.

With the debate now concluded, the Republican who wins the primary later this month will go on to run in the state’s Nov. 3 general election against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews — a race that’s projected to heavily favor the GOP. The primary, set for Aug. 11, will likely decide which Republican will go on to win a full six-year term in November.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Why Trump is downplaying reports Russia and China are helping Iran
summary: Trump says he'll ask Putin directly about satellite imagery allegations as experts warn Russia and China are quietly aiding Iran against U.S. forces.
story: Reports indicate China is supplying Iran with shoulder-launched missile systems through Pakistan and raising concerns about potential threats to U.S. aircraft. Lt. Col. James Carafano (ret.) talks President Trump's war approach on 'Varney & Co.'

President Donald Trump cast doubt in recent days on allegations that Russia is helping Iran target U.S. forces, even as members of his own administration acknowledge Moscow and Beijing are supporting Tehran in other ways.

Trump dismissed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that Russia supplied Iran with satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf, saying any assistance would have been "very unimpactful" given the damage inflicted on Iran's military.
"We’ll find out if that’s true. I’ll ask Putin. We’ll find out," Trump told reporters at the end of July.
WALTZ WARNS OF CHINESE, RUSSIAN-FUELED ‘NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT’ LOOMING CLOSE TO US SHORES
President Donald Trump cast doubt in recent days on allegations that Russia is helping Iran target U.S. forces.  (Al Drago/Getty Images)
"I don’t think they’ve been doing it, certainly not at a high level," Trump added. "And if they have, it has been very unimpactful."
Trump pointed to the damage Iran’s military has suffered during the war. Russian help, he argued, has failed to stop the United States from destroying much of Tehran’s conventional forces.

Trump's comments came as his administration confronted separate reports that Russia and China are helping Iran in different ways — allegations that, if borne out, would suggest America's two chief geopolitical rivals are quietly supporting a nation at war with the U.S. Members of his own administration have acknowledged broader help from Moscow and Beijing.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has said Russia and China are "enabling some of the things Iran is doing," but a White House official told Fox News Digital that any foreign assistance has failed to improve Tehran's ability to attack Americans.

Trump's comments came in response to two recent reports: Zelenskyy's allegation that Russia provided satellite intelligence to Iran and a Reuters report that China could send hundreds of shoulder-fired air-defense missiles to Tehran through Pakistan, which China has denied.
Fresh satellite imagery could help Iran locate high-value assets and refine strike coordinates, then show whether an attack hit its intended target.

"As the President stated, nothing that any outside actor is doing to help Iran is in any way increasing their ability to target Americans," the official told Fox News Digital, responding to questions about Zelenskyy's claim that Russia gave Iran satellite imagery of U.S. military installations in the Gulf.

Zelenskyy laid out Ukraine's evidence Saturday, saying Russian satellites had surveyed Gulf countries and U.S. military installations beginning in early July before the imagery later appeared in Iran.
"These images subsequently appear in Iran," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Ukraine found what Zelenskyy described as a "clear correlation" between the Russian observations and subsequent Iranian attacks. According to Zelenskyy, Moscow collected imagery before strikes to aid targeting and returned afterward to assess the damage.

Zelenskyy said Russian satellites focused on four air bases over two days — two in Bahrain and one each in Jordan and Kuwait — and said Ukrainian intelligence had shared the information with foreign partners.

Ukrainian Ambassador to the U.S. Olga Stefanishyna said at a July 30 reporter roundtable that the allegation did not arise during Zelenskyy’s White House meeting with Trump because the agenda was crowded. She said Ukraine had provided the information "through other channels."
A Ukrainian official told Fox News Digital that Kyiv wants to avoid "opening a second front" with Iran.
Iran conducts joint military exercises with Russia in the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. deployed surveillance drones. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Hegseth acknowledged Russian and Chinese support for Iran during a Senate hearing in July.
There was "definitely adversary alignment," Hegseth said. Russia and China were "at different levels, enabling some of the things Iran is doing."

The U.S. has ways to deter that support, he added, though some of those measures should remain classified. Hegseth said earlier in the war that the administration knew "exactly" what Moscow and Beijing were doing and was addressing their actions where needed.

Russia has denied supplying Iran with intelligence on American military targets. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the locations of U.S. bases were publicly available. The Kremlin also dismissed earlier reporting about Russian intelligence support for Iran as false.

Trump also questioned reports that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan, saying Chinese President Xi Jinping had assured him Beijing would stay out of the conflict.

"That was surprising. I mean, things like that happen, but that would be surprising. He told me very strongly he wouldn’t partake, but he knows I’d be quite disappointed. He’s coming here, I think, on September 24," the president told reporters Wednesday.
Matthew Kroenig, a former Pentagon and intelligence official, called the reports "highly plausible," pointing to growing cooperation among Russia, China and Iran.
"From Russia and China’s point of view, if they can complicate the U.S. war in the Middle East and raise the cost to Washington, that’s a good thing for them," Kroenig told Fox News Digital.

Smoke rises from Wildberries facility, from what the Ukrainian authorities say was following a drone attack, in Shushary, Pushkinsky District, St. Petersburg, Russia, July 24, 2026, in this screen grab taken from a social media video. (SOCIAL MEDIA/via Reuters)
Kroenig said Trump may be warning Moscow and Beijing privately instead of confronting them before television cameras.
"That might be the most generous interpretation, that it’s his way of warning China and Russia to knock it off," he said.

Trump’s comments would carry more risk if the president were relying on assurances from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kroenig said. He urged the administration to make clear that either country would face a cost for helping Tehran.
"I think there would be a risk to just discounting this altogether," Kroenig said.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said Moscow has spent years building closer military ties with Tehran.
"If this proves accurate, Russia has found a way to help Iran without direct military engagement, and that’s why this is significant," Borshchevskaya told Fox News Digital.
Iran began supplying Russia with Shahed attack drones in 2022, giving Moscow a cheap weapon it could launch in waves against Ukrainian cities and power infrastructure.

Russia later began producing its own versions with Iranian support and improved the design, making the drones a mainstay of its attacks. Tehran’s earlier support now hangs over Zelenskyy’s claim that Moscow is helping Iran target American forces.
Satellite imagery would give Moscow another way to aid Tehran while avoiding a direct clash with American forces.
"It’s hard to think how the provision of intelligence is insignificant," Borshchevskaya said.
She said Trump may be trying to keep his public exchanges with Moscow calm as U.S. officials send firmer messages in private.

Russia views the wars in Ukraine and Iran as connected parts of its campaign against American influence, Borshchevskaya said. U.S. officials tend to handle each conflict through a separate policy process.
"The challenge for us is that we often separate theaters, but Russia does not," she said. "Russia looks at all of these conflicts in a much more interconnected way."
Borshchevskaya said Russia has chosen forms of aid that can strengthen Iran without committing Russian troops or entering a direct fight with Washington.
"Russia is being restrained here," she said. "They’re playing a much more nuanced game."
Trump also voiced surprise Wednesday at a report that Iran could soon receive hundreds of Chinese-made, shoulder-fired air-defense systems through Pakistan.
Xi had given Trump a firm assurance that China would stay out of the war, according to the president.
"He told me very strongly he wouldn’t partake, but he knows I’d be quite disappointed," Trump said.
China called the report "groundless." Pakistan rejected the claim that it would help route the weapons to Iran, calling the allegation "baseless and devoid of truth."
A soldier operates a drone jammer MANPAD, similar to the air defense weapon China is reportedly selling to Iran. (Liesa Johannssen/Reuters)

Kroenig said Beijing has supplied Russia with economic and industrial support during the war in Ukraine. China has stopped short of openly sending lethal weapons, a limit he had expected Beijing to observe in the Iran war.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Advanced air defenses would require approval from the Chinese government, he said. Russian satellite intelligence would also come from state-controlled capabilities.
"There are no mom-and-pop shops in St. Petersburg selling this data," Kroenig said.

title: Socialist insurgents eye Midwest gains as Dem civil war threatens must-hold Senate seat
summary: Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens clash in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history, with over $80 million spent and AIPAC at the center.
story: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan takes questions from Fox News in the final stretch ahead of Tuesday’s high-stakes primary in the Great Lakes battleground state.
DETROIT, MI - The high-stakes fight between the left-wing and the center-left establishment for the future of the Democratic Party is front-and-center on Tuesday in Michigan's primary.

Boosted by a string of victories this spring in mostly blue congressional districts across the country, the Democrats' ideological war moves to the Great Lakes battleground state, where progressive victories could reshape the party and endanger must-hold seats in the midterm elections.

Also at stake as Michigan joins Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington State in holding mid-summer primaries is President Donald Trump's immense clout over the GOP and the power of his endorsements in Republican nominating contests.
But taking top billing is Michigan's divisive and expensive Democratic Senate primary, which is seen as the biggest stage to date in the fierce fight for the future of the Democratic Party.
THE MIDTERM SENATE RACES THAT COULD FLIP THE BALANCE OF POWER IN CONGRESS

"This is ground zero in the battle for the future of the Democratic Party, pitting status quo corporate Democrats against shake up the system economic fighters, and we’ll see who wins," Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC), a leading group on the left, told Fox News Digital.

The primary face-off pits Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County Health Department director, against Rep. Haley Stevens, a more moderate candidate backed by the establishment. The race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, who is backing Stevens, is a must-hold for the Democrats and one of roughly a dozen Senate races from coast to coast that will determine if Republicans hold onto their slim Senate majority.

Matt Bennett, one of the leaders at the Third Way, a leading center-left Democratic organization, told Fox News Digital the Michigan showdown is "the first time the left is competing for a swing seat" and warned, "the significance is it could really put this seat in jeopardy."

El-Sayed, who, if elected, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator, is an epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018. He has made support for "Medicare-for-all" a major component of his campaign.

The far-left candidate has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and is a vocal critic of Israel amid its war with Hamas — even characterizing Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide" against Palestinians.
MIKE ROGERS ARGUES ABDUL EL-SAYED IS 'A SPECIAL SAUCE OF CRAZY'
Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, speaks to supporters at a campaign event on Aug. 2, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

And El-Sayed, who is backed by top far-left leaders and teamed with progressive champions Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York on the Michigan campaign trail two weeks ago, and who served as a top surrogate on Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign, has vowed not to accept PAC donations.

Stevens, who flipped a GOP-held district in her 2018 election to Congress, is backed by top national and Michigan Democrats, including Peters, term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and longtime Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.
Schumer and the party establishment view Stevens as more electable than El-Sayed, who has sparked controversy with his past comments.

"I am the best Democrat to go forward. I am the only person in this race who has won tough primaries multiple times. You know, running with the Michigan grit, resilience and determination," Stevens told Fox News Digital on Sunday, as she teamed up with Peters on the campaign trail.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and retiring Sen. Gary Peters, at a campaign rally on Aug. 2, 2026, in Madison Heights, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Over $80 million has been spent on the primary showdown, making it the most expensive Democratic Senate nomination race in history. Much of the money has been shelled out by outside groups in support of Stevens and against El-Sayed. The biggest spending comes from United Democracy Project, a political action committee aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

El-Sayed, who has repeatedly attacked Stevens over the massive infusion of AIPAC-linked money, told reporters on Sunday, "If you need $70 million to come in here and help get you elected, then the question has to be, are you actually electable on your own terms."
The winner will face off in the midterms against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, who is on a glidepath to win the GOP Senate nomination.
The Trump-backed Rogers, who lost the 2024 Senate election in Michigan by a razor-thin margin, said in a Fox News Digital interview that he doesn't care whom he faces off with in November.
"It doesn't matter to us. We've looked at both candidates. We feel confident we're going to beat either one of those candidates that come out of that race," Rogers highlighted.
And Rogers claimed, "They are very radical, and they are way too extreme for Michigan. I mean, Abdul, he has his own special sauce of crazy."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
But Democrats are confident they can regroup after a combustible primary.

"Let's make sure that anyone but Mike Rogers gets to the United States Senate," Stevens told reporters on Sunday. "After the primary, you're going to see a united Democratic Party. You are going to see us going full force, full fledged ahead."
And El-Sayed told Fox News Digital, "I think we all understand the risk of Donald Trump. We all understand the risk of Mike Rogers."

The left-wing versus establishment battle is also playing out in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, a key Republican-controlled swing seat race that's among roughly two-dozen that will impact whether the GOP holds onto its fragile House majority.

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, which advocates for political action to tackle climate change, is on the rise against two more moderate Democrats. Lawrence is backed by Sanders and El-Sayed, as well as some top progressive groups. The primary winner will face GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in the general election.
The party civil war is also on display in Michigan's deep blue 13th Congressional District.
MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS
Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney rallied over the weekend in his bid to unseat Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., on Aug. 2, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

title: Federal judge blocks New York law banning ICE agents from wearing masks
summary: A federal judge temporarily blocked New York from enforcing a law requiring ICE and other federal agents to remove masks and display identification during operations.
story: White House 'border czar' Tom Homan discusses California Gov. Gavin Newsom's law banning masks for law enforcement, the deportation operations and responds to bribery allegations on 'The Ingraham Angle.'

A federal judge on Monday blocked key portions of a New York law that would have prohibited federal immigration agents from wearing masks and required them to display visible identification while carrying out their duties.

U.S. District Judge Mae D'Agostino of the Northern District of New York issued a preliminary injunction preventing the state from enforcing the two provisions while a legal challenge to the law continues to move forward.

In her ruling, D'Agostino found the challenged provisions were likely unconstitutional because they interfere with federal law enforcement operations, including those carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
FIRST ON FOX: DOJ SUES SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA OVER LAWS KNEECAPPING FEDERAL AGENTS AS MASK WAR ESCALATES
FILE - Federal immigration agents may continue wearing masks while on duty after a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of a New York law. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy, File)

The judge said only the federal government has the authority to establish policies governing federal law enforcement operations. Therefore, New York cannot dictate how federal agents perform their official duties.
"New York cannot impose its own uniform requirements on federal agents simply because it disagrees with how the Federal Government is exercising its authority," the ruling stated.
Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James criticized the court's decision to block the mask ban, saying they are currently reviewing more legal options.
DEM GOVERNOR IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER TESTING LIMITS OF AUTHORITY WITH MAJOR MOVE AGAINST ICE

FILE - U.S. District Judge Mae D'Agostino ruled New York likely exceeded its authority by trying to regulate how ICE, the FBI, DEA and CBP agents carry out federal law enforcement duties. (Will Waldron/Albany Times Union)

"While the court enjoined enforcement of New York’s mask ban, we stand firm in our belief that masked agents do not make New York safer and our offices are reviewing all legal options at this time," the pair said in a joint statement.
However, D'Agostino declined to block a separate provision barring New York local law enforcement agencies from performing certain federal immigration enforcement functions under 287(g) agreements.
FILE - New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks at a press conference, July 31, 2024, in the Bronx borough of New York. (Julia Nikhinson/AP Photo)
The judge said participation by state and local agencies in federal civil immigration enforcement is voluntary under federal law.

"The State's refusal to cooperate in the immigration context—a possibility contemplated by the relevant federal statutes—does not constitute discrimination against the federal government," the ruling stated.

New York Attorney General Letitia James (pictured) said she and Gov. Kathy Hochul are reviewing additional legal options after a federal judge blocked key portions of a New York law banning federal immigration agents from wearing masks. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hochul and James welcomed that portion of the ruling, saying New York taxpayers should not have to fund local cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

"As we have said from the start, New York’s ban on 287(g) agreements is legal and will keep our communities safe. Local law enforcement should be focused on local matters, and New York taxpayers should not have to foot the bill for any collaboration with ICE," their statement read.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: 'The Brink of War' tells story of Reagan-Gorbachev nuclear discussions
summary: Jeff Daniels stars as Ronald Reagan in "The Brink of War," a film about the Reykjavik summit that paved the way for the historic INF Treaty.
story: Fox News anchor Bret Baier previews ‘The Brink of War,’ which explores the historic summit between former President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in Iceland, on ‘Special Report.’

President Ronald Reagan met with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev five times in the late 1980s. The first such meeting was in Geneva, Switzerland in November 1985 when the two leaders began to form a relationship. It was the second meeting in Reykjavik, Iceland, where Reagan and Gorbachev began to find trust.

"The reason I wanted to do it really, truly, was because I think these days we've gotten so good at yelling at one another that we are not talking anymore," said "The Brink of War" director Michael Gunn. "What blew me away about the story when Secretary Schultz told me about it was that these were two guys who had every reason to hate each other, had every reason to be enemies, and they sat down in a room together and tried to make a better world."
US RAMPS NUCLEAR WEAPONS PRODUCTION TO COLD WAR LEVELS AS CHINA PURSUES ‘UNPRECEDENTED’ BUILDUP
Jeff Daniels stars as President Ronald Reagan in "The Brink of War," a film centered on the 1986 Reykjavik summit with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. ("The Brink of War" / Angel Studios)

Jeff Daniels stars as Reagan in "The Brink of War," which follows the Reykjavik summit with Gorbachev, played by Jared Harris. Reagan's Secretary of State George Schultz, played by J.K. Simmons, was instrumental in giving Gunn behind-the-scenes details for his film.

"We spent hours and hours together. I interviewed him. He gave me the declassified transcripts that informed the script. He's a hero of mine. The movie is dedicated to him, for him, for his public service," Gunn said.
NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY CHRONICLES 20-YEAR JOURNEY BEHIND ‘REAGAN’ FILM
"The Brink of War" explores how Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev built trust during nuclear arms negotiations in Iceland. ("The Brink of War" / Angel Studios)

"The Brink of War" not only highlights the Reagan administration's ambitions for peace but also their disappointments. One scene shows Reagan’s doubt over trusting Gorbachev amid the negotiations as Schultz assures him it was not the end of talks to find common ground between the two global powers.
"This moment where they figured out just the two of them in a room that they could trust one another, I think led to all that. The first arms reduction agreement in human history," Gunn said.

While no final agreement was reached in Iceland, the summit paved the way for several more meetings between Reagan and Gorbachev. It also led to several peace treaties — like the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (INF), which required both sides to liquidate a class of nuclear weapons.
PRESIDENT TRUMP'S NEGOTIATING TEAM PRAISED BY NUCLEAR EXPERTS FOR WALKING AWAY FROM PAKISTAN TALKS
Director Michael Gunn says Reagan and Gorbachev’s willingness to keep talking offers a lesson for leaders confronting conflicts today. ("The Brink of War" / Angel Studios)

"For the first time on the highest level, we and the Soviets came close to an agreement on real reductions of both strategic and intermediate-range weapons," President Reagan said after his meeting with Gorbachev in Iceland. "We were in sight of an historic agreement on completely eliminating the threat of offensive ballistic missiles by 1996. I can help remembering being told just a few years ago. Radical arms reduction was an impossible dream, but now it's on the agenda for both sides."
Gunn believes the Reagan and Gorbachev's discussions should be an inspiration for ending today's conflicts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think the lesson for today is that we have to continue dialog," Gunn said. "As tough as it gets, I want people to walk out of the theater with hope that if we engage, if we're strong, if we are seeking peace in a genuine way and we find a genuine partner that we can make a better safer world even today."
"The Brink of War" debuts in theaters Aug. 14.

Baier is also host of FOX News Audio's "The Bret Baier Podcast" which includes Common Ground and The All-Star Panel. title: Democrats blink as Schumer helps GOP clear key shutdown hurdle
summary: Chuck Schumer endorsed the continuing resolution as Senate Republicans race to clear a government funding bill before leaving Washington, D.C.
story: Montana Congressman Ryan Zinke discusses the House's passing of the Reconciliation 3.0 framework, concerns over the lack of spending offsets, the passing of the NDAA with the SAVE America Act included. Zinke also comments on government funding approaches amid a looming shutdown.
Senate Republicans opted to strike on bipartisan momentum and take a key step to prevent a government shutdown almost two months before the deadline.

The upper chamber voted in a bipartisan wave to clear the first procedural hurdle for a short-term funding extension that would see the government open through the midterm elections and into early December.
It comes after Republicans have spent months hand wringing that Democrats would again shut the government down to score political points during the pivotal November elections.
HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and the GOP are gearing up for a floor battle with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats over Trump-backed voter ID legislation. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The actual deadline to fund the government is not until Sept. 30, when the current fiscal year expires, but Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that it’s better to move now then to wait to create more "certainty" in the coming weeks.

"There's been enough uncertainty this last year, and, you know, unfortunately, I think through two government shutdowns that extended for a long period of time, it's better for everybody if there's predictability, certainty," Thune said.
Congress has been no stranger to shutdowns during President Donald Trump’s second term, with two of the longest in history taking place under Republican control of the legislative branch.
SENATE WEIGHS NEW, PAINFUL LEVERAGE TACTIC AS FEARS OF ANOTHER GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN GROW

The first happened last year, and entered the record books as the longest full government closure that stretched over 40 days. That battle was over now-expired Obamacare tax subsidies, an issue that was never fully reconciled in the months that followed.

Then came the shutdown earlier this year that stretched for over 70 days. Democrats rebelled against a bipartisan funding deal after Renee Nicole Good was slain in Minnesota by immigration enforcement agents. That prompted Republicans to skirt Democrats entirely and fund immigration enforcement on their own.
But, for now, there is a bipartisan current pushing through the Senate to at least make sure a shutdown doesn’t happen for the time being.
SCHUMER BACKS GOP'S PLAN TO BRING THE PAIN DURING FUTURE SHUTDOWNS: 'I'M GOING TO VOTE FOR IT'
The 2026 midterms will determine control of the House and Senate, shaping President Donald Trump's legislative agenda during the final two years of his term. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., endorsed the continuing resolution (CR) on Monday, arguing that the current bipartisan offering was the "responsible path forward that allows continued bipartisan negotiations on a budget that delivers for American families."
"For months, Democrats have been clear: we want to fund the government, avoid a shutdown and pass strong, bipartisan appropriations bills that improve people’s lives," Schumer said in a statement.

Republican leadership is hopeful that they can clear the decks and advance the CR to the House during the Senate’s last official week in town before jet-setting from Washington, D.C., back to lawmakers' respective home states.
While the CR is the current top priority, there are several other items waiting in the wings, too.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There’s a package of over 70 nominees Republicans want to ram through, the long-awaited Russia sanctions package, a crypto market structure package that, for now, appears doomed, and the final confirmation vote for acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump’s pick to lead the Department of Justice (DOJ).
"I think we have a bunch of stuff we have to finish and we’ll just stay until we finish it," Thune said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: ‘Doctor’ El-Sayed’s bizarre health hustle raises campaign headache: ‘Moon Juice Brain Dust’
summary: Abdul El-Sayed criticized Mehmet Oz for selling health products as a doctor, then used his own medical credentials to promote supplements and devices.
story: Fox News contributor Joe Concha vehemently criticizes Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for allegedly misrepresenting his medical credentials. Concha highlights the rigorous path and sacrifice of real doctors, contrasting it with El-Sayed's claims. He argues El-Sayed, lacking a medical license, has not saved lives, branding his claims as deceitful and a disservice to the profession. Concha argues voters should be wary of such misrepresentations.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed made money promoting health products, including while invoking his medical credentials, despite saying he broadly rejected advertisements for products making health claims and criticizing others for doing the same.

Before running for Senate, El-Sayed hosted a podcast that provided him with a six-figure income partially through ad reads. Among the companies El-Sayed promoted for cash, often citing his purported experience as a doctor, were firms selling supplements, peptides, and an Israeli metabolism-tracking device that has been scrutinized by health experts.
The ad reads came despite an assurance from El-Sayed that he would not use his platform to sell health products to people who listen to him.
SOCIALISM'S WAR ON SUCCESS HAS A NEW CHAMPION — AND HE’S RUNNING FOR SENATE IN MICHIGAN
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed poses for a portrait in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Saturday, Feb. 21, 2026. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
"I broadly reject any advertisements that are for products making claims about health," he wrote in a now-deleted social media post from March 2022.

El-Sayed also accused Mehmet Oz during his 2022 Pennsylvania Senate run of being part of the "medical industrial complex that exists to sell you things that you don’t need that are not actually based in any level of science."
"Yet he can … say, ‘Well, I’m a doctor, so you should trust what I have to say,'" El-Sayed added.
DR OZ REVEALS THE HEALTHY RETIREMENT HABIT THAT COULD MAKE AMERICA $1 TRILLION RICHER

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), Michigan Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) greet the crowd after El-Sayed spoke at The People V. The Powerful rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
After assuring his audience that he wouldn't hawk health products, and criticizing Oz for using his medical credentials for doing so, El-Sayed used his medical credentials to sell health products.

"Even as a doctor and epidemiologist, nutrition labels are obnoxiously hard to process," El-Sayed said during a March 2025 ad read. "That's where Thrive Market comes in. See, I love Thrive Market, my go to online grocery store for getting all of my healthy essentials delivered. And I don't even have to leave my couch."

Thrive Market has sold a wide selection of supplements, including items such as "Moon Juice Brain Dust" and "Royal Jelly Brain Fuel" that claim to improve the cognitive function of those who use them. Health experts have cast doubt on whether or not such supplements can actually improve brain function.

Moon Juice Brain Dust describes itself as a "nootropic blend of adaptogens and herbs that target stress to support mental stamina, alertness, and concentration" that is "informed by Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda." Royal jelly, meanwhile, is a thick, milky substance produced by bees to feed their queen. Proponents argue it can be helpful in treating menopause symptoms or addressing low energy, though scientific evidence for such claims is limited.
Thrive did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.
IV THERAPY AND SUPPLEMENTS UNDER SCRUTINY AS EXPERTS WARN OF POTENTIAL SIDE EFFECTS
Michigan Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at The People V. The Powerful rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

While El-Sayed has leaned heavily on his identity as a doctor both in doing ad reads and on the campaign trail, public records indicate that he never held a medical license or completed a residency. He does, however, hold a medical degree and a doctorate degree in public health.
The New York Post was the first to report on El-Sayed’s advertisement for health goods.
A company making moon dust and brain jelly wasn’t El-Sayed’s only customer.
On July 23, 2024, El-Sayed read an ad promoting a medical device created by an Israel-based startup.

"Lumen is the world's first handheld metabolic coach. It's a device that measures your metabolism through your breath and on the app. It lets you know if you're burning fat or carbs and gives you tailored guidance to improve your nutrition, workout, sleep, and even manage your stress," he said. "All you've got to do is breathe into your Lumen first thing in the morning, and it'll give you an inside look into what's going on with your metabolism, whether you're burning mostly fats or carbs."
Years before El-Sayed took Lumen’s advertising money, experts were raising concerns about its medical claims.

"I just don’t see a practical use for the product in helping people achieve their weight-loss goals," Harbor-UCLA Medical Center senior researcher Nicholas Tiller told Outside Magazine in 2022. "The use of metabolic flexibility and other science-sounding terms lend the product a false scientific legitimacy."
"It’s quintessential marketing over science," he added.
