title: License plate cameras are tracking drivers everywhere
summary: The DeFlock map displays about 119,000 license plate readers across the U.S., with Flock Safety cameras accounting for 83% of the mapped total.
story: Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker and Criminal Defense Attorney Josh Ritter discuss the use of AI-powered license plate readers. Parker notes their utility in law enforcement investigations, citing Miami Beach's successful implementation. Ritter, referencing the Supreme Court's "Shattery" ruling on geofencing, expresses concern about mass data collection without warrants.

One minute, you are driving to the grocery store. The next, a camera above the road photographs your car and adds the sighting to a searchable database. You probably will not hear a click or see a flash. In fact, you may never notice the camera mounted on a pole near the intersection.

Automated license plate readers have quietly spread across the country. As of our reporting, the open-source DeFlock map displayed about 119,000 readers across the United States. DeFlock is a community-powered project that maps reported camera locations using public submissions and data from OpenStreetMap. Because the map relies partly on crowdsourced information, it may miss some cameras or include locations that have changed.

Flock Safety cameras account for about 83% of the mapped total. California has the largest number of mapped readers, with more than 16,000. Major clusters appear around Los Angeles and the Bay Area. Police say the cameras help locate stolen cars and vehicles connected to serious crimes.
FLOCK SURVEILLANCE SPREADS ACROSS THE SOUTH AS RED-STATE LAWMAKERS SEEK TO AX '1984'-STYLE TRACKING TOOLS
A solar-powered Flock Safety camera shows how roadside surveillance hardware can blend into the landscape while watching vehicles pass. (Flock Safety)

However, privacy advocates warn that the same network can reveal where ordinary people travel throughout the day. Each sighting can include a vehicle's plate number, appearance, location and the time it passed the camera. Flock says its system can search by plate, vehicle type and visible features.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
Why license plate cameras are appearing everywhere

Automated license plate readers, also known as ALPRs or LPRs, have become common tools for police departments. Businesses and homeowners associations can also install them. The rules can vary depending on who owns the camera and who gets access to the data.

The cameras often appear on poles near streets, intersections and neighborhood entrances. Some have solar panels attached to the pole. As a car passes, the camera takes a photograph. Software reads the license plate and turns the image into a searchable record. CyberGuy previously found that license plate cameras are also scanning vehicles at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots.

Flock Safety has become one of the largest vendors in this market. Its cameras connect to a cloud-based system where authorized customers can review vehicle sightings. Unlike red-light cameras, these readers generally focus on identifying vehicles. They typically do not issue traffic tickets. Still, every passing vehicle can enter the database. The driver does not need to face suspicion or have any connection to an investigation.
What license plate cameras capture about your car

A reader begins with your license plate number. However, the record can include much more than the characters printed on the plate. The system records a vehicle's make and model. It can also note the color and body type.

Visible features may become searchable as well. These can include a roof rack, bumper sticker or missing hubcap. The record also includes the camera location and a timestamp. Together, those details show where the vehicle appeared and when it passed. Flock says its license plate reader system focuses on vehicles rather than faces. The company also says its LPR cameras exclude facial recognition and biometric identification.
Your daily drive can become searchable data

A single camera sighting may reveal little about your day. Several sightings can start to form a pattern. For example, a vehicle that appears near the same house each evening may reveal where someone lives. Another record could show a visit to a medical provider.

A license plate can also connect a car to information held by a state motor vehicle agency. That connection can help investigators identify the registered owner. Authorized personnel can search for a complete plate number. They may also search using a partial plate or vehicle description.

A department looking for a dark SUV with a roof rack could receive several possible matches. Investigators would then need to confirm which vehicle they want. That search ability can save time during an urgent case. Meanwhile, it also gives agencies access to information about drivers who have done nothing wrong.
Where the license plate camera network is growing

California leads the country with more than 16,000 mapped readers, according to an analysis of DeFlock data. Florida followed with 7,169 cameras. Georgia had 7,046. Illinois had 5,822. The concentration becomes clearer when the figures are compared with road mileage. San Francisco County ranked third nationwide with 1,196 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Only New York County and Kings County ranked higher.
In Southern California, Orange County ranked No. 33 nationwide. It had 184 cameras per 1,000 road miles. Los Angeles County ranked No. 59 with 143 cameras per 1,000 miles.

However, DeFlock cannot provide a complete camera inventory. The open-source project relies on public reports and data from other sources. As a result, populated communities may have more markers because more people submit camera locations. Rural areas may appear less covered even when readers exist there. A missing marker cannot guarantee that a road has no camera. Likewise, some mapped locations may need updates after a camera moves or disappears.
How police use license plate camera data

Police departments can place license plates connected to stolen vehicles on a hotlist. They may also add cars linked to active investigations. When a camera detects a matching plate, the system can alert officers. That may help them locate a stolen car or find a missing person's vehicle. Investigators can also search earlier sightings. Those records may show where a vehicle appeared before or after an incident. However, an automated alert still requires human verification.

A recent LAPD review examined more than 210 million plate scans over two months. The system incorrectly flagged 161 plates as stolen. Yet not every incorrect alert led to a police encounter. During the same period, 337 alerts helped officers recover stolen vehicles. Those results show both the investigative value and the risk of an incorrect match.
Why privacy advocates are raising alarms

License plate readers collect information from millions of vehicles. Most belong to people with no connection to a crime. Privacy advocates say connected camera networks can create a detailed driving history without requiring a warrant. They also worry about access by agencies far from the community that installed the camera.

Those concerns have already affected ordinary drivers. CyberGuy reported on a Colorado woman who was wrongly accused after Flock camera records linked her truck to the area of a porch theft. She had to gather Google Location Timeline data, vehicle camera footage and other evidence to prove where she had been. Police later voided the summons and dropped the case.
California restricts where ALPR data can go

California law limits how local law enforcement agencies share automated license plate reader information. The state prohibits local agencies from giving ALPR data to federal authorities or out-of-state agencies. State officials say the information must remain within California.

However, allegations of improper sharing have raised questions about whether every agency follows those restrictions. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued the city of El Cajon in October 2025. His office accused the city of sharing ALPR data with more than 100 out-of-state law enforcement agencies.

In January 2026, Bonta asked a court to order the city to stop the sharing. The case remained part of California's effort to enforce its ALPR privacy laws. The dispute highlights a gap between written policy and technical enforcement. A rule may prohibit sharing, but the system also needs controls that block unauthorized access.
THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

A Flock Safety-branded license plate reader camera site on a lamppost near the intersection of Peacock Drive and Bristol Road in Ventura on Sept. 9, 2025. (Isaiah Murtaugh/The Star/USA Today Network via Imagn Images/Reuters)
LAPD pauses Flock access after agreement expires

The Los Angeles Police Department entered a three-year operating agreement with Flock Safety in 2023. The arrangement covered access to data from 138 pole-mounted cameras across the city. The agreement expired on July 11, 2026. LAPD allowed it to lapse while officials addressed concerns involving data ownership, privacy and security. The department also wanted clearer limits on how Flock could store, share and use information collected by the cameras.

The 138 cameras continued operating after the agreement ended. However, LAPD employees no longer had regular access to the data they collected. That information remained stored in the cloud and could become available to investigators if the city finalizes a new agreement. Police officials began negotiating proposed terms with stronger safeguards. Under those terms, the city would retain ownership of every image, record and piece of metadata captured by the cameras.

Flock would also be prohibited from selling, publishing or sharing the information with outside organizations. In addition, the company could not use the data for commercial purposes or to train artificial intelligence systems. As of our reporting, LAPD and Flock had reportedly not finalized a replacement agreement, and talks are believed to be ongoing.

LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell called the technology a valuable investigative tool. Still, he said the department needed to use it responsibly. The dispute shows how quickly a camera program can raise difficult questions about control and oversight. Those questions become harder to resolve after a large network has already begun collecting information.
What Flock Safety says about driver privacy

Flock rejects claims that its license plate readers continuously track a vehicle. The company says each camera captures a vehicle at one specific location. However, authorized agencies can search separate sightings stored within the system.

Flock says its default retention period lasts 30 days. Customers may choose a different period based on local laws or contract terms. The company also says customers control their information and sharing settings. According to Flock, every search is connected to a specific account and recorded in an activity log.

However, access questions can become more complicated when public-records laws enter the picture. CyberGuy previously reported that a Washington judge ruled Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records, even when a private company stores the files for a city. The decision did not mean every driver record would automatically become public. However, it showed that using an outside vendor may not remove government surveillance data from state transparency laws.

Flock also says it does not sell customer data or use facial recognition with its LPR cameras. It says automated deletion and annual security audits help confirm that agencies follow their selected retention periods. Those safeguards address part of the privacy debate. Yet their effectiveness depends on how each customer configures the system and reviews employee activity.
What license plate cameras mean for you
You may never receive a notification when a license plate camera records your vehicle. Still, you can learn more about the readers operating around your community.

Check DeFlock at deflock.org for reported cameras near your home and regular driving routes. Remember that public submissions help build the map. Therefore, it may contain gaps or outdated locations. Look for cameras mounted high on narrow poles. A nearby solar panel can also signal a roadside reader.

Search your city or police department website for its ALPR policy. The policy may explain how long the department keeps vehicle records. It should also describe the types of investigations that allow a search. Do not assume every agency uses Flock's 30-day default. Contracts and local rules can set a shorter or longer retention period.

Find out whether other departments can search your community's camera data. A city may have strict internal rules while sharing access with a much larger network. That wider access can make local safeguards harder to evaluate. Look for an agency transparency portal if one exists. You can also request a list of connected departments from your city.

City council agendas often reveal proposed camera purchases before installation begins. Search meeting documents for terms such as "ALPR," "automated license plate reader" or "Flock Safety." Contract documents may show how many cameras the city plans to install. They can also explain who will own the records. Public meetings give residents a chance to ask questions before officials approve a larger network.

Ask who reviews searches for possible abuse. Audit logs offer limited protection when nobody checks them. You should also find out what happens after an employee violates the policy. Departments should explain whether they suspend access or begin an investigation. Strong consequences can discourage personal searches. They also show whether an agency treats its privacy rules seriously.

A close-up view shows an automated license plate reader camera mounted at a Lowe’s store in Connecticut, where the technology can capture vehicle plate data as shoppers drive by. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

License plate readers can help police find a stolen vehicle or develop leads after a serious crime. That explains why departments, businesses and homeowners associations continue installing them. Still, these cameras record everyday drivers who have no connection to an investigation. A series of sightings can reveal where you go and when, even though the camera never captures your face. The Colorado case shows what can happen when a camera record points police toward the wrong person. Meanwhile, the Washington ruling raises another concern because some images held for a city may qualify as public records. Flock says customers control their data and can review searches through activity logs. Those protections depend on departments limiting access, checking for misuse and enforcing their own policies. LAPD's decision to pause access after its agreement expired shows that privacy concerns can slow a major camera program. However, the ongoing talks suggest the technology will remain part of the public safety debate. Before more cameras appear, your community deserves clear answers about who can search the records, how long the data stays available and what happens when someone abuses access.

Would you accept license plate cameras throughout your community if police said they helped solve crimes, or has this type of tracking already gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Don't let fake election websites fool you before 2026 midterms
summary: Over 62,000 election-named domains were tracked since September 2025, with some active storefronts copying campaign branding to collect donations.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You spot a campaign shirt online that makes you laugh. The site carries the candidate's name. It also has polished product photos and a familiar checkout page. So, you assume the store supports the campaign.
A fake election website can copy enough campaign cues to make that assumption feel reasonable. Your money and personal information could then reach an operator with no verified campaign connection.

New research provided to CyberGuy by WhoisXML API, an internet intelligence company that analyzes domain, IP and DNS data, tracked 62,081 election-named domains created since September 2025. Researchers identified 13,645 addresses that read like campaign sites based on their names.

The research classifies only a portion of the domains as campaign-style addresses. Legitimate campaigns, supporters, merchants and domain investors may control many of them. However, researchers also found live storefronts that used candidates' names while selling merchandise and accepting donation-style payments. That smaller group creates the clearest risk for you.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Voters should verify campaign websites, donation links and committee disclaimers before entering personal or payment information. (Getty Images)

Why fake election websites surge before the midterms

National elections create a rush for online real estate. Campaign teams want memorable web addresses before someone else claims them. Supporters may launch fan pages, while merchants see an opportunity to sell political products. Impersonators can follow the same naming formula.

According to WhoisXML API, nearly 46% of the curated campaign-style set used structures such as "[name]for[office]" or "for[state]." Domains referencing congressional races appeared most often. Senate-themed names came next. State names also appeared across about one-third of the curated set. Texas led with 537 registrations. Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Colorado followed.

Those names feel familiar because real campaigns use the same structure. As a result, a questionable domain can look credible before you open the page. Across the domains studied, researchers said 90% hid the registrant's identity. In addition, 88% carried a one-year registration term. Privacy protection and short registration terms can have legitimate uses. Still, those details deserve more attention when a new site also copies campaign branding or asks for money.
How fake election websites copy real campaign stores

A small change in a domain can hide in plain sight. WhoisXML API highlighted massiemoneybomb[.]us, which closely resembled the established massiemoneybomb[.]com fundraising address. The main difference appeared after the final dot.

That change may look obvious on a large computer screen. However, it becomes easier to miss on a phone, especially when a text or social media post opens the page directly. Researchers also examined kenpaxton[.]us. They said the domain was 58 days old when captured, while kenpaxton[.]com dated back to 2008.

The newer site reportedly sold supportive campaign products alongside merchandise criticizing the same candidate. That unusual mix offers a clue that the store may lack an official connection. Yet many shoppers will focus on the product photos or the price. A polished checkout can make the entire operation feel established. Alexandre François, the WhoisXML API domain scam researcher behind the study, told CyberGuy that AI can help operators build convincing websites quickly and at scale. That makes it even harder to judge a campaign page by its appearance alone.
How fake election donation pages collect personal data

Political merchandise may cost you more than the price on the screen. According to the research, some storefronts allowed visitors to add donation-style payments of up to $1,000 to a shopping cart. The sites then processed the payment through their own checkout flows.

One store reportedly continued accepting a donation-style payment after the candidate's official ActBlue page stopped taking contributions. The checkout requested a full name, street address, email address and phone number. It also collected payment card details.

A familiar payment processor can make that form feel safe. However, its presence only shows how the payment moves through the checkout. It cannot confirm that the candidate authorized the store or that the campaign receives the money.

François said the study found no direct evidence that donors lost money or had their data misused. "Only the payment platforms could see whether a donor lost money or had data misused, and their data was not part of this study," he told CyberGuy. The findings support caution rather than a claim that every highlighted site committed fraud.
What domain records reveal about fake election websites

Domain registration records can expose useful clues before or after a website launches. Researchers can review the creation date, registrar, paid registration period and privacy status. Sometimes, the records also identify the owner or registrant country. However, each clue has limits.

Many legitimate website owners use privacy services to keep home addresses and contact details out of public databases. Campaigns may also register several defensive domains so impersonators cannot claim them first. A one-year registration term also appears across ordinary websites. Price and convenience often drive that choice.
The risk grows when several details point in the same direction. A nearly copied domain may lead to a new storefront with an unofficial donation flow. A mismatched disclaimer adds another concern.

For federal political committees, public websites generally need a disclaimer that identifies who paid for the communication. The wording may also state whether a candidate authorized it. The FEC explains that disclaimer requirements cover political committee websites and online fundraising communications. A disclaimer cannot guarantee honesty. Still, a missing or mismatched statement gives you a strong reason to leave the page and verify the site elsewhere.

Campaigns also face limits when trying to secure every possible variation of a candidate's name. François said they should consistently promote one official domain and one donation link. He added that "the realistic option is monitoring" because registering every possible look-alike domain would be impractical. Monitoring new registrations can help campaigns find look-alike sites during their first days online. Campaigns can then report suspicious pages to the registrar, hosting company or payment provider.
SAME-NAME CANDIDATE DISQUALIFIED FROM KEY SENATE RACE OVER ALLEGED DEM SCHEME TO CONFUSE VOTERS
Fake election websites, like the one pictured, can copy campaign branding, storefront designs and donation pages to collect money and personal information. (WhoisXML API)
Ways to stay safe from fake election websites
Before you buy campaign merchandise or make a political contribution online, use these checks to confirm that the site connects to the candidate or committee you intend to support.

Avoid starting with a link from an unexpected text, email, online ad or social media comment. Instead, search for the candidate independently. Then compare the result with links from the candidate's verified social media account or established public profile. "No single sign is enough, so it's best to check a few together and to reach the page from the campaign's own channel," François told CyberGuy.

You can also use a personal data removal service to reduce the personal information available through data brokers and people-search sites. This may limit the details scammers can use to make unexpected messages, targeted ads or social media comments feel more convincing. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

For federal races, use the FEC's campaign finance database at fec.gov/data/ to look up candidates and registered committees. The database shows federal candidate and committee filings. For state or local races, check the appropriate state or local election authority. Many campaigns process contributions through ActBlue or WinRed. In those cases, the payment address should show secure.actblue.com or secure.winred.com. Some campaigns use other processors, so an unfamiliar payment provider alone does not prove the page is deceptive.
Tap or click the address bar before entering payment information. Check the spelling and domain ending. Then look for added words or letters that imitate the campaign's real address.

A scammer may replace ".com" with ".us." Another operator may add words such as "official," "store," "donate," or "support" to make the address feel authentic. François said the difference may also involve one word, a hyphen or an ending such as ".vote" or ".store."

Scroll to the bottom of the site and review the area around the donation form. A federal political committee website should identify who paid for the communication. Depending on the committee, the disclaimer may also explain whether the candidate authorized it.

Compare that committee name with the FEC database. Leave the page when the names conflict or the disclosure looks vague. Keep in mind that a deceptive page can copy a real committee's name. Treat the disclosure as one clue rather than proof that the page belongs to the campaign.
Open the candidate's established website in a separate tab. Look for a direct link to the merchandise store or donation page. If the official site sends you somewhere else, use the link it provides.

Also review the store's contact details and return policy. Be cautious if it sells products supporting a candidate alongside merchandise attacking that candidate. That unusual mix may signal the store has no official campaign connection. A page that keeps collecting contributions after a candidate withdraws also deserves closer scrutiny. The same applies when a store continues selling campaign merchandise after the official donation page closes.
The padlock in your browser means the site uses an encrypted connection. It offers no proof about the person or business behind the page.

CISA warns that phishing attacks may use malicious websites that impersonate trusted organizations to collect personal information. A professional design and secure connection still require you to verify the operator.
Pressure can push you past obvious warning signs. Be cautious when a site claims a donation match will disappear within minutes. A countdown clock that keeps resetting should also raise concern.
The FTC's broader donation-safety guidance recommends researching an organization and resisting pressure to give immediately.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Researchers found campaign-style websites selling political merchandise and accepting donation-style payments under candidates’ names. (yasindmrblk/Getty Images)

A credit card generally offers stronger dispute protections than a debit card. It also keeps the payment away from funds in your checking account. The FTC says legal protections for credit cards exceed those for debit cards in billing disputes.

Save your receipt and take screenshots of the product page and checkout. Make sure the full domain appears in at least one image. After you pay, check your statement to confirm the amount and make sure the site did not enroll you in recurring contributions.

A fake campaign website may try to push a malicious download or send you to another harmful page. Strong antivirus software can help detect suspicious files and block some dangerous websites. However, you still need to verify the campaign connection before you pay. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

If a store asks you to create an account, use a unique password. A password manager can generate and save a strong password for you, so you do not have to remember it. Reusing a password could put your other accounts at risk if the login information gets exposed. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) when the site offers it.
What to do after paying through a fake election website

Contact your card issuer or bank as soon as you suspect a problem.Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse the transaction. The FTC advises consumers who paid a suspected scammer by credit or debit card to contact the issuer and request a reversal.Next, report suspected fraud through the FTC's ReportFraud system. If the site may have violated federal campaign finance law, you can also review the FEC complaint process.The FEC accepts complaints about possible violations involving federal election financing. Its authority covers elections for the U.S. House, Senate and president.Watch your statements for unfamiliar charges. Also change any password that you reused on the store.If the website collected information that later appears in identity fraud, IdentityTheft.gov can create a recovery plan and guide you through the next steps.
Contact your card issuer or bank as soon as you suspect a problem.
Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse the transaction. The FTC advises consumers who paid a suspected scammer by credit or debit card to contact the issuer and request a reversal.
Next, report suspected fraud through the FTC's ReportFraud system. If the site may have violated federal campaign finance law, you can also review the FEC complaint process.
The FEC accepts complaints about possible violations involving federal election financing. Its authority covers elections for the U.S. House, Senate and president.
Watch your statements for unfamiliar charges. Also change any password that you reused on the store.
If the website collected information that later appears in identity fraud, IdentityTheft.gov can create a recovery plan and guide you through the next steps.
Kurt's key takeaways on fake election websites

Election season gives questionable websites a powerful disguise. A candidate's name can create trust before you verify who operates the page. The scale of this research should make every online donor slow down. Researchers found more than 62,000 election-named domains, though many may serve legitimate purposes. The clearest concern comes from active storefronts that copy campaign-style branding and collect money outside a verified campaign path. Take an extra minute before buying a shirt or making a contribution. Find the official campaign site through a trusted source. Then confirm the web address and committee disclosure before you enter personal or payment information.

title: Washington man arrested on arson charge tied to devastating Spokane wildfire
summary: A man was arrested and charged with arson on Monday in connection with the Old Trails Fire in the Spokane area in Washington state, police said.
story: Fox News’ Sarah Alegre reports on wildfires across Spokane County, Washington, destroying hundreds of structures and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate on ‘Special Report.’

A Washington state man was arrested Monday on a first-degree arson charge in connection with the Old Trails Fire, one of several wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate the Spokane area, authorities said.

Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, was taken into custody after Spokane County Sheriff’s Office detectives and Washington Department of Natural Resources investigators developed probable cause to arrest him, according to the sheriff’s office.

Citizen tips and information from Airway Heights police officers and Spokane County sheriff’s deputies who responded to the initial call and conducted evacuations helped lead investigators to Farinacci, the sheriff’s office said.
Authorities described Farinacci as a convicted felon from Arizona but said they had found no documented criminal history involving fires.
Investigators have not connected Farinacci to the two other major blazes burning in the area, the Autumn Lane and Fairview fires, officials said.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT
Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged with first-degree arson. (Spokane County Sheriff’s Office)
"We will be looking into any other crimes Mr. Farinacci may have committed in the past," Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said during a news briefing.
Nowels said first-degree arson was the charge supported by probable cause at that stage of the investigation and cautioned that the case could change as authorities gathered additional evidence.
Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Farinacci and a search warrant for his residence in the 2800 block of West Elliott Drive, according to the sheriff’s office.
Deputies served the warrant Monday and arrested Farinacci without incident. Authorities said detectives found a butane lighter and waterproof matches while detaining and searching him.
SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH
Firefighters respond to wildfires near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)
Farinacci was booked into the Spokane County Jail and was being held on $1 million bond.

The Old Trails Fire was first reported Saturday near North Old Trails Road and West Euclid Road. It became the largest of three destructive fires burning around Spokane and remained uncontained Monday, according to authorities and wire reports.
Wildfires rage in Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue)

The three fires had collectively destroyed at least 700 structures and prompted evacuation orders affecting approximately 67,000 people as of Monday, according to The Associated Press. More than 1,000 firefighters were battling the blazes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency Saturday amid drought, unusually high temperatures and strong winds. The declaration also imposed a statewide prohibition on most outdoor and agricultural burning through Sept. 30.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Pennsylvania school bus aide accused of sexually assaulting special needs teen
summary: A Pennsylvania bus aide faces indecent assault and child endangerment charges after allegedly inappropriately touching a special needs student.
story: The father of the Georgia school shooter, Colin Gray, is sentenced to 15 years in prison. Legal analyst Donna Rotunno joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the historic sentencing precedent and parental responsibility.

A Pennsylvania school bus aide was arrested after he allegedly inappropriately touched a 14-year-old girl with special needs and appeared to take photographs and videos of her with his cellphone, according to police.
Ali Khan, 62, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors, indecent assault and related offenses, the Bensalem Township Police Department said.
Khan was being held at the Bucks County Correctional Facility after failing to post 10% of his $500,000 bail.
The girl’s parents contacted police on Thursday, July 30, to report that their daughter had allegedly been inappropriately touched by a bus aide earlier that day, according to investigators.
HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP
Ali Khan, 62, was arrested for inappropriately touching a special needs teenager. (Bensalem Township Police)

Police said their investigation determined that Khan allegedly touched the Bensalem High School student multiple times on Wednesday, July 29, and Thursday, July 30, while she was riding a bus to the school’s extended school year program.

Investigators said surveillance footage from inside the bus showed Khan directing the girl to a specific seat before allegedly touching her inappropriately while securing her seatbelt and after she was seated.
Police said the footage also appeared to show Khan engaging in sexual conduct and using a cellphone to photograph or record the girl.
Ali Khan was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors and indecent assault. (Google Maps)

"Bensalem Police would like to commend the victim of this assault for having the courage to come forward and report the assault," police said. "Additionally, Bensalem Police would like to thank the Bensalem School District for their assistance with this investigation. The safety and well-being of our students continues to be the top priority of both the Bensalem Township Police Department and the Bensalem School District."
The Bensalem Township School District said the employee was immediately removed from service and from the district pending the outcome of criminal and administrative investigations.

"The safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority," the district said in a statement. "Whenever concerns involving student safety are brought to our attention, we act immediately to protect students, support families, and cooperate fully with law enforcement. We are committed to conducting a thorough administrative review while respecting the integrity of the criminal investigation."
CALIFORNIA MIDDLE SCHOOL ASSISTANT PRINCIPAL NABBED IN CHILD SEX STING
The footage showed Ali Khan putting his hand inside his pants and touching himself during the encounter. (Bensalem Township Police)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The district is fully cooperating with the Bensalem Township Police Department and will continue to assist law enforcement as requested. The district will also continue its own administrative investigation in accordance with Board policy, district procedures, and applicable law," the statement added.
Khan’s preliminary hearing is scheduled for Aug. 11, 2026.
The incident remains under investigation.

title: Lindsay Clancy defense scores ‘extremely helpful’ psychosis concession as expert flags next hurdle
summary: A hospital psychiatrist agreed that Lindsay Clancy could plan and communicate while psychotic, a key concession in the Duxbury murder trial.
story: Jurors weigh evidence in the case of the Duxbury mother accused of strangling her three young children.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney sought to blunt prosecutors’ portrayal of the Massachusetts mother as organized and calculating, pressing a hospital psychiatrist to acknowledge that a person can communicate, make plans and carry them out while experiencing psychosis.
"People can communicate and plan and act on plans even if they’re in the middle of a psychosis, right?" defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Dr. Sejal Shah Monday.
HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
"Yes," Shah replied.

Defendant Lindsay Clancy on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, the fifth day of testimony at Plymouth Superior Court for her murder trial. Clancy is charged with three counts of murder in connection with the death of her three young children in 2023 at their Duxbury home. Clancy says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and is not criminally responsible. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Reddington then asked whether someone must be "drooling and stumbling and unable to walk and talk" to be psychotic. Shah said no and agreed that a person in psychosis can still communicate with others.

Clancy is charged in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, inside the family’s Duxbury home. Her defense maintains she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
Dr. Sejal Shah testified she examined Clancy multiple times at Boston’s Brigham and Women’s Hospital in January and February 2023. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Seth J. Zuckerman, a celebrity criminal defense attorney, former New York City prosecutor and founder of Zuckerman Legal Group, said the case will turn on Clancy’s mental state at the precise time the children were killed.
"What was in her mind at the exact time that she killed her children?" Zuckerman told Fox News Digital.
He said prosecutors have focused on Patrick Clancy’s trips to CVS and a local restaurant, along with his communications with his wife, to portray her as lucid during the critical time frame.
WATCH: Psychiatrist calls Lindsay Clancy an 'honest' patient
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL
Shah, an associate chief of psychiatry and medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, first evaluated Clancy five days after the killings.
She testified that Clancy was confused, made mistakes during a cognitive assessment and had experienced visual hallucinations after spinal surgery.
Shah diagnosed delirium and said possible causes included anesthesia, oxygen problems and an elevated heart rate. The symptoms resolved by the following day, Shah said.

Prosecutors argued in opening statements that Lindsay Clancy "deliberately and meticulously" killed her children and "acted intentionally, rationally and swiftly to accomplish a very specific goal." (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
During later evaluations, Clancy appeared calm and cooperative, displayed organized and goal-directed thinking and denied hallucinations and suicidal or homicidal intent.
Reddington used cross-examination to argue those observations did not establish Clancy was free of psychosis at the time of the killings.
"Was she, in your opinion and your experience, an honest patient telling you what her symptoms were, if any?" Reddington asked.
"Yes," Shah said.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"She didn’t go off and try to exaggerate to you and say, ‘I’m seeing visions, and I’m hearing voices,’ and suicidal ideation and homicidal ideas," Reddington said. "She didn’t say any of those things to you, did she?"
"Correct," Shah said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"So this is not, in your opinion, someone who was trying to exaggerate her conditions for some legal reason, correct?" Reddington asked.
"No," Shah replied.

Zuckerman called that concession "extremely helpful to the defense," although not decisive.
"They want to portray her as someone who wasn’t manipulative, who didn’t have some grand plan," he said.
Lindsay Clancy appears in court Monday in Plymouth, Massachusetts. She has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder for the killings of her children. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
SEND US A TIP
On redirect, prosecutors challenged the defense’s portrayal by focusing on Clancy’s medication history.
Shah agreed Clancy was not taking every psychiatric medication discussed at the same time and said she had not known some prescriptions were barely used or untouched.
GOT A TIP?

Shah also confirmed that Clancy requested do-not-resuscitate status after surviving her fall from a second-story window. The hospital did not immediately change her status because of the reported suicide attempt.
Shah said Clancy later agreed her mental health should be stabilized before reconsidering the request.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Zuckerman said Monday’s cross-examination helped the defense by supplying testimony that Clancy could appear lucid at some moments while experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms at others.
Still, he said its value will depend on whether the defense can connect those symptoms to the moment the children were killed.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"The burden is on the prosecutors to show that she was criminally responsible at the time of the deaths," Zuckerman said. "That is unique to Massachusetts, and I think it’s beneficial to the defense here."

On January 24, 2023, Clancy fatally strangled her three children in the basement of their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home using exercise resistance bands. She then cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window in a suicide attempt, leaving her partially paralyzed. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation. Judge William Sullivan told jurors that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when the children were killed.

title: California mom begged for help before ex gunned her down in front of their 4-year-old son: DA
summary: Jeffery Kendall was sentenced to 50 years to life for fatally shooting Brittany Ligdis during a 911 call as their 4-year-old son watched in Pinole.
story: More than two years after prosecutors said Jeffery Kendall fatally shot Brittany Ligdis in front of their 4-year-old son, a judge sentenced him to 50 years to life. Credit: KTVU

More than two years after a California mother's desperate 911 call ended with her 4-year-old son witnessing her killing, the father prosecutors said carried out the execution will spend decades behind bars.

Jeffery Kendall, 39, was sentenced Monday to 50 years to life in prison for murdering 30-year-old Brittany Elizabeth Ligdis just 10 days after she ended their relationship, according to the Contra Costa County District Attorney’s Office.
A jury found Kendall guilty in May of first-degree murder and child endangerment for placing the couple’s young son in a situation that threatened his safety.
DISPATCHER HEARD 'LOUD BANG' BEFORE TIKTOK INFLUENCER WHO OUTED ALLEGED PEDOPHILE HUSBAND FOUND DEAD: AUDIO
Booking photo of Jeffery Kendall following his arrest in the Brittany Ligdis murder case. (KTVU)
Prosecutors said Ligdis called 911 on the morning of Feb. 16, 2024, after Kendall broke into her Pinole home while she hid in a laundry room with their 4-year-old son.
About 90 seconds into the call, Kendall entered the room.
"Let go of me," Ligdis pleaded, according to the district attorney’s office. "You're scaring him."
DECADES-OLD COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLINGS OF MARRIED COUPLE BEFORE CHILD
Law enforcement officers place Jeffery Kendall in handcuffs following his arrest in Santa Cruz, California. (California Highway Patrol)
Moments later, she screamed, "Stop it," before Kendall shot her in the head, prosecutors said.
The couple’s son cried out, "Momma," and fled the room while Kendall ran from the home. Responding officers found Ligdis dead from a gunshot wound to the head.

Deputy District Attorney Tylyn Wells described the killing as "an execution in front of a 4-year-old child" and argued it was not the result of "a mental break," according to the district attorney’s office.
ALABAMA MOTHER SENTENCED TO LIFE FOR HIRING HITMAN TO KILL HER CHILD'S FATHER OVER CUSTODY DISPUTE
A law enforcement officer escorts Jeffery Kendall through a police facility after his arrest. (California Highway Patrol via FOX 2 San Francisco)
Instead, Wells said the murder reflected a pattern often seen in domestic violence cases, where the danger escalates after a victim decides to leave.
Wells asked the court to impose a sentencing enhancement that increased Kendall’s punishment to 50 years to life.
Contra Costa County Superior Court Judge Glenn Kim called the case "one of the most difficult" he had experienced before imposing two consecutive terms of 25 years to life.
Kim also barred Kendall from contacting his son, with limited exceptions subject to court approval, until November 2035, when the boy turns 16.
Separately, Judge Kim convicted Kendall of illegally possessing a 3D-printed semi-automatic pistol and determined that multiple factors supported a harsher sentence.
One year after Brittany Ligdis' death, her mother shared an emotional video urging family and friends to remember her daughter's life rather than the violence that ended it.
Brittany Ligdis smiles while holding her young son in a family photograph taken before her death. (KTVU)

title: ICE detainee who illegally re-entered US after deportation dies at Delaney Hall
summary: Edwin Jovanny Lopez-Cornejo died at Delaney Hall detention facility in New Jersey after a medical emergency, sparking calls from Gov. Sherrill to close it.
story: Lawmakers clash at a House Judiciary Committee hearing over immigration enforcement and conditions at New Jersey's Delaney Hall Detention Center. Bill Melugin reports as Republicans reject what they call ‘false narratives’ about ICE's treatment of detainees, while Democrats point to alleged inhumane conditions and hunger strikes at the facility on ‘Special Report.’

A 41-year-old Salvadoran national who re-entered the United States illegally has died in federal custody after being arrested in New Jersey following a previous deportation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials announced Monday.
Edwin Lopez-Cornejo died Aug. 1 at University Hospital in Newark after suffering a medical emergency while detained at the Delaney Hall Detention Facility, according to an ICE statement.
Staff with the GEO Group, the private detention company that manages the facility, along with medical personnel, responded to the emergency and called 911.
The official cause of death remains pending a formal medical examination, according to ICE.
SOROS-BACKED NONPROFIT ACCUSES NJ GOV SHERRILL OF SPREADING 'MAGA PROPAGANDA' ON ICE DETAINEES

ICE agents stand guard in front of protesters outside the federal immigration center at Delaney Hall in Newark, where ICE is housing detained immigrants on May 26, 2026, in Newark, New Jersey. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Lopez-Cornejo was first apprehended by U.S. Border Patrol for entering the U.S. without inspection on or about Aug. 13, 2006.
A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered him removed on Aug. 25, 2006, and he was deported to El Salvador on Oct. 19, 2006.
He later re-entered the U.S. illegally on an unknown date before ICE officers arrested him in Plainfield, New Jersey, on June 18.
He was held at Delaney Hall pending removal pursuant to the reinstatement of his prior removal order.
ICE officials said that Lopez-Cornejo received proper medical care during his detention.
MORE THAN 100 HAITIAN IMMIGRANTS WITH VIOLENT OFFENSE AND SEX CRIME CONVICTIONS DEPORTED: DHS
Protesters, politicians and ICE agents gather outside Delaney Hall, an immigration facility in Newark, N.J., on May 27, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)
The agency notified the Department of Homeland Security oversight offices, the Consulate of El Salvador in Elizabeth, and Lopez-Cornejo's next of kin, the statement said.
Lopez-Cornejo's death drew swift condemnation from New Jersey officials, who reiterated demands to shut down Delaney Hall.

"I am deeply disturbed to hear of a detainee death inside Delaney Hall this weekend," New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said in a statement. "My heart is with the individual's loved ones, who deserve answers about what happened. My administration is working with our congressional delegation to gather all the facts surrounding this death."
NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR, DEMOCRATIC SENATOR SPEND MEMORIAL DAY PROTESTING ICE FACILITY
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said she was "deeply disturbed" to hear of Edwin Lopez-Cornejo's death. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"This tragedy is another painful reminder of why Delaney Hall should be closed," Sherrill added.
Newark Mayor Ras J. Baraka also issued a statement condemning the incident.

"In less than a year, yet another family is forced to endure the unimaginable loss of a loved one while in custody at Delaney Hall," Baraka said. "The death of Edwin Jovanny Lopez-Cornejo is a heartbreaking reminder of the consequences of a facility that has operated for far too long without adequate oversight, accountability or transparency."
Another detainee, Jean Wilson Brutus, 41, died Dec. 12, 2025, after suffering a medical emergency less than 24 hours after entering the facility.

The New Jersey facility has repeatedly been accused by state and local inspectors of obstructing health and safety inspections and has been the site of ongoing protests and detainee hunger strikes over food quality, overcrowding and medical care.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

title: Illegal immigrant who helped torch CHP cruiser during LA anti-ICE riot learns his fate
summary: An illegal immigrant who poured lighter fluid onto a burning CHP cruiser during the Los Angeles anti-ICE riots was sentenced to 37 months in federal prison
story: New footage reveals Andrew Arapaca setting a fire outside the Manhattan Federal Building, a site for immigration courts. The suspect, with known anti-immigration and Customs Enforcement activity, used an incendiary device. This dramatic event has prompted an FBI investigation, with further details anticipated as authorities probe the motives behind the attack in New York City.

An illegal immigrant who prosecutors say poured lighter fluid onto a burning California Highway Patrol cruiser while officers were trapped beneath a Los Angeles freeway overpass during last year's violent anti-ICE riots is headed to federal prison, becoming the latest person convicted in the brazen attack.

Yachua Mauricio Flores, a 23-year-old Mexican national living in Los Angeles' Lincoln Heights neighborhood, was sentenced Monday to 37 months in federal prison and ordered to pay $253,415 in restitution for his role in the June 8, 2025 riot, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Federal prosecutors said Flores stood on the Main Street overpass above U.S. Highway 101 as officers below were bombarded with rocks, chunks of concrete, fireworks, street signs, burning debris and other objects hurled by rioters.
FORMER MARINE GETS 100 YEARS IN PRISON AS JUDGE CALLS ICE DETENTION CENTER AMBUSH 'AN ASSAULT ON DEMOCRACY'

Federal evidence image shows prosecutors say Yachua Mauricio Flores pouring lighter fluid from the Main Street overpass during the June 2025 anti-ICE riots in Los Angeles. (United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California)
As a CHP cruiser burned beneath the overpass, Flores poured lighter fluid from two separate bottles onto the flames, causing the fire to intensify, according to court records.
Prosecutors said he then directed another rioter to pour a flaming liquid onto the vehicle before helping throw an electric scooter over the railing toward CHP officers and patrol vehicles below.

Booking photo of Yachua Mauricio Flores, the Mexican national sentenced in connection with the June 2025 Los Angeles anti-ICE riots. (United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California)

Flores admitted he knew officers were trapped beneath the overpass and acknowledged that hurling heavy objects and burning debris created a substantial risk of death or serious bodily injury, according to his plea agreement. He pleaded guilty in April to one count of obstructing, impeding and interfering with law enforcement officers during a civil disorder.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Burning debris falls from a Los Angeles freeway overpass as California Highway Patrol officers respond below during the June 2025 anti-ICE riots. (United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California)

"Violent attacks on law enforcement will result in federal prison time," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. "Those who escalate chaos and endanger officers will be held accountable. Today's sentence reflects our commitment to protecting the men and women sworn to keep our communities safe."

A California Highway Patrol vehicle with a shattered windshield after officers came under attack during the June 2025 anti-ICE riots in Los Angeles. (United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California)
The attack unfolded two days after violence erupted during federal immigration enforcement operations in Los Angeles, leading to days of anti-ICE riots across the city.
Federal prosecutors have charged seven people in connection with the Main Street overpass attack, alleging several worked together to target the CHP cruiser and the officers trapped beneath it.
3 SUSPECTS INDICTED IN ASSAULT OF TPUSA REPORTER SAVANAH HERNANDEZ DURING MINNEAPOLIS ICE PROTEST: SOURCES

A CHP vehicle burns beneath the Main Street overpass in downtown Los Angeles during anti-ICE riots on June 8, 2025, after rioters targeted officers below, according to federal prosecutors. (The United States Department of Justice)

According to court records, Flores, Ismael Vega, 42, and Adam Charles Palermo, 40, all helped drop burning debris toward the cruiser while other rioters hurled rocks, chunks of concrete, fireworks and other objects at officers attempting to clear the overpass.

Flores is the latest person sentenced in the case. Vega received the same 37-month prison sentence last week after admitting he helped ignite burning debris that prosecutors said Flores later intensified with lighter fluid.

Palermo, who prosecutors have described as the lead participant in the attack, is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 14 after pleading guilty to assaulting, resisting and impeding people assisting federal officers with a deadly or dangerous weapon. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison.
Following Monday's sentencing, Essayli highlighted the case in a post on X.
"Another day, another illegal immigration rioter from last summer is sent to federal prison," Essayli wrote.

"Actions have consequences. Those who attack law enforcement will face the full force of justice. This defendant can now reflect on his actions from a federal prison cell."
The FBI investigated the case with assistance from the California Highway Patrol and the Los Angeles Police Department.

title: Trump administration's immigration push fuels ICE's biggest arrest month in agency history
summary: ICE averaged roughly 1,645 immigration arrests per day in July, smashing June's record of 43,000 as new funding and personnel fuel the crackdown.
story: Bill Hemmer and Chad Wolf analyze ICE plans to surge arrests of Haitian migrants, focusing on temporary protected status. They examine CBP nationwide encounter numbers for Haitians under the Biden administration, totaling nearly 500,000. Wolf highlights the Democratic Party's major shift on border security, referencing past statements from Barack Obama and current calls to abolish ICE.

The Trump administration's immigration crackdown reached a historic milestone in July as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement made roughly 51,000 immigration arrests, setting the highest monthly arrest total in the agency's history.
ICE averaged approximately 1,645 immigration arrests per day during the month, according to multiple federal sources who spoke with Fox News.
The historic total came just one month after ICE set what was then a new monthly record with roughly 43,000 arrests in June, giving the agency back-to-back record-breaking months.
TRUMP DHS CHIEF UNDER FIRE FROM CONSERVATIVES AFTER IMMIGRATION SPEECH IGNITES BACKLASH
ICE arrested more than 100 illegal alien truck drivers in California’s Operation Highway Sentinel following deadly crashes tied to state-issued CDLs. (Department of Homeland Security)
Federal sources told Fox News the surge followed a slowdown in ICE arrests in the weeks and months after unrest in Minneapolis.

They attributed the record-setting pace to the end of the Department of Homeland Security shutdown, thousands of newly hired ICE personnel hitting the streets and billions of dollars in new funding from two reconciliation bills that replenished the agency's coffers.
The additional money is helping fuel expanded hiring and enforcement operations nationwide, according to the sources.
ICE NABS ILLEGAL ALIENS CONVICTED OF CHILD SEX CRIMES AND METH TRAFFICKING IN NATIONWIDE ENFORCEMENT SWEEP
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference, July 1, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/David 'Dee' Delgado)
The Department of Homeland Security praised ICE officers in a post on X Monday, highlighting the agency's efforts to arrest and remove criminal illegal immigrants.
"Every day, the brave men and women of ICE are arresting and DEPORTING dangerous criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, from our country," DHS wrote.
"Under @POTUS Trump and @SecMullinDHS, the safety of the American people will always come first," the department added.
TOM HOMAN WARNS ICE SURGE COMING TO NEW YORK CITY AS MAMDANI BOASTS ABOUT SANCTUARY STATUS
The record-setting month comes as ICE has ramped up high-profile enforcement operations across the country. (Courtesy Charles Reed/U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement via Reuters)
The July figures represent the highest single-month arrest total ever recorded by ICE and mark the second straight month the agency has broken its own record.
The record-setting month comes as ICE has ramped up high-profile enforcement operations across the country under the Trump administration.
Last month, ICE announced its Harlingen, Texas, field office arrested 238 illegal immigrants in a single day, setting a record for targeted arrests in the Rio Grande Valley.
According to the agency, those taken into custody included a suspected Paisas gang member and a Mexican national previously convicted of attempted kidnapping, sexual battery and illegal reentry.
At the time, ICE Harlingen Field Office Director Juan Agudelo said the agency remained focused on "enhancing public safety and restoring integrity to our nation's immigration system."

title: Manhattan DA's office says Luigi Mangione defense spread false claims about murder trial media plan
summary: Prosecutors accuse Luigi Mangione's defense team of spreading misinformation about media access plans for his upcoming Manhattan murder trial.
story: Defense attorneys representing Luigi Mangione demand a live broadcast of his upcoming murder trial, arguing that media limits violate his Sixth Amendment rights. Fox News' Todd Piro breaks down the new court filings detailing three defense objections.

Manhattan prosecutors asked a judge Monday to correct what they called false claims by Luigi Mangione's defense team about media access to his upcoming murder trial and remind the attorneys of their ethical obligations.

The filing came days after Mangione's lawyers argued the court's plan for public and media access violates his constitutional right to a public trial and alleged the Manhattan District Attorney's Office was involved in deciding which reporters would be allowed to cover the proceedings.
Prosecutors denied the allegation, saying the office "had no role" in developing the New York State Office of Court Administration's media access plan or selecting journalists to cover the trial.
MANGIONE LAWYERS SAY MEDIA LIMITS AT MURDER TRIAL ARE UNCONSTITUTIONAL, FEAR COURT WILL 'HAND-PICK' PRESS

"The defense's baseless accusation thus appears to be nothing more than an attempt to spread misinformation about this case and delegitimize the proceedings," Senior Trial Counsel Joel J. Seidemann wrote in a letter to Judge Gregory Carro.
Luigi Mangione appears in court in Manhattan for a pretrial evidence hearing on Dec. 11, 2025. (William Farrington for New York Post via Pool)

The Manhattan District Attorney's Office asked Carro to remind Mangione's attorneys of their ethical obligations not to knowingly make false statements to a court or third parties, citing New York's Rules of Professional Conduct.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

In Friday's filing, defense attorneys Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan argued the court's media access restrictions amount to a partial closure of the proceedings in violation of the First, Sixth and 14th Amendments.
TYLER ROBINSON ASKS FOR MORE SECRET HEARINGS AFTER LOSING FIGHT OVER CAMERAS IN COURT
The attorneys objected to the lack of an overflow courtroom, limits on jury selection coverage and what they described as a process allowing only a select group of reporters to attend the trial.

Luigi Mangione appears at a pre-trial hearing in Manhattan Criminal Court on June 17, 2026. Mangione is accused of murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in December 2024. (Pool via Barry Williams for New York Daily News)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

They also claimed they were told only 68 journalists would receive general access to the proceedings and that the selection process had effectively been outsourced to a private attorney representing several legacy media organizations.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Mangione's attorneys asked the court to hold a public hearing, identify the journalists selected to cover jury selection and the broader trial, explain how those reporters were chosen and detail efforts to secure an overflow courtroom.
They also asked the court to either broadcast the proceedings live or explain why that would not be permitted.
Luigi Mangione arrives at an evidence suppression hearing at the Manhattan Supreme Court in New York City, May 18, 2026. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters via Pool)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Prosecutors responded Monday that the defense had wrongly implicated the district attorney's office in decisions made by the Office of Court Administration.

"The District Attorney's Office had no role in developing the Office of Court Administration's media access plan for this trial, and will have no role in selecting which news reporters attend the trial, as defense counsel surely knows from her long prior association with this office," Seidemann wrote in the filing.

Mangione's attorneys then fired back Monday in a response to the DA's office's letter, saying prosecutors had misunderstood their position. They insisted they are not claiming the Manhattan District Attorney's Office helped shape the court's media access plan.

Instead, they said they want a hearing to determine whether the DA's office, including its press office, communicated with the Office of Court Administration (OCA) about restrictions on press and public access in this case.

The defense acknowledged it has no firsthand knowledge that any such communications took place in Mangione's case. However, the attorneys argued they know from decades of experience working in the Manhattan DA's Office that prosecutors' press office has routinely coordinated with OCA and court security on media logistics in other high-profile cases.

As an example, they pointed to the 2017 Etan Patz murder case, saying the DA's press office worked with OCA to coordinate media access for prosecutors' post-verdict news conference. They said they are not offering that as proof similar coordination occurred here, but as evidence that the issue warrants a hearing.
Mangione's attorneys also rejected prosecutors' request that the judge remind them of their ethical obligations, calling the accusation "unfounded and deeply ironic."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

They pointed to allegations they have previously raised during suppression hearings, including claims prosecutors listened to a privileged phone call between Mangione and his attorneys, obtained his medical records using what they described as a subpoena listing a fictitious court date and recorded Mangione while he was alone in an interview room at the Altoona Police Department without a court-ordered wiretap.

They also renewed their claim that prosecutors have refused to correct what they say was a false statement made by NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny, who publicly claimed Mangione's mother said the alleged killing "might be something that she could see [her son] doing."

The defense again asked Carro to hold a hearing and order the preservation of any emails, text messages or other communications between the DA's office and OCA regarding press and public access to the case.

Mangione is charged in New York state court with murder and terrorism-related offenses in the Dec. 4, 2024, fatal shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel. He has pleaded not guilty.

title: HEAR IT: Mom's frantic 911 call after thief steals Instacart driver's car with toddler inside
summary: Body camera video and 911 audio reveal the frantic 15-minute rescue of a 2-year-old from a stolen car during an Instacart delivery in Atlanta.
story: Body camera video captures the tense moments officers surround a stolen vehicle and arrest the suspect accused of driving away with a 2-year-old child still inside. Credit: Atlanta Police Department

A routine Instacart delivery turned into every parent's nightmare after a Georgia mother's car was stolen with her 2-year-old daughter still inside, as newly released 911 audio and police body camera video capture the frantic rescue.
"Someone just stole my car and it has my 2-year-old daughter in it," the distraught mother tells an Atlanta 911 dispatcher in audio released by police.

When the dispatcher asks whether the child is inside the vehicle, the mother replies, "Yes, my 2-year-old daughter was in the backseat. I was dropping off an Instacart order and I came back outside and my car is gone. My daughter was inside."
HELICOPTER FOOTAGE CAPTURES FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY ABANDONING CHILD DURING HIGH-SPEED CHASE FROM DEPUTIES
Atlanta police officers surround a stolen vehicle after tracking it down with license plate readers during the rescue of a 2-year-old girl. (Atlanta Police Department)
Moments later, she cries out again, "My daughter was inside!"
The ordeal unfolded around 4:36 p.m. on July 30, according to the Atlanta Police Department.
Police said the vehicle had been left running with the toddler inside while her mother delivered an Instacart order.
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

Officers with the department's Auto Crimes Enforcement Unit immediately began searching for the vehicle and used the city's license plate readers to locate the car, the suspect and the child in under 15 minutes, according to police.
Body camera video released by the department shows officers surrounding the stolen vehicle and ordering the driver to raise his hands and get out.
"Hands up! Hands up!" an officer shouts.
MIKE WALTZ, TIM TEBOW LAUNCH EFFORT TO COMBAT ONLINE CHILD EXPLOITATION: 'IT'S HAPPENING IN THEIR BACKYARD'
Atlanta police body camera video shows officers handcuffing Saleem Martin after locating a stolen vehicle with a toddler inside. (Atlanta Police Department)
"Hands on the window now," another officer orders. "What you're gonna do is you're going to get out and face away from me, you understand me? Get out the car, slow. Put your hands behind your back."
The video shows officers taking the suspect into custody as the toddler cries nearby and her mother works to calm her.
"It's okay, baby. It's okay, baby," the mother can be heard saying.
Moments later, an officer radios, "The child is okay. The child's okay."
Police identified the suspect as 21-year-old Saleem Martin.
Mugshot of Saleem Martin, who faces kidnapping and other charges after police say he stole a vehicle with a toddler inside. (Atlanta Police Department)
Martin was charged with kidnapping, theft by taking, simple battery, entering an automobile, cruelty to children and criminal attempt to commit a felony, according to police.
Authorities said the toddler was unharmed and reunited with her parents.
According to an arrest warrant obtained by Atlanta NBC affiliate 11Alive, the child's mother later noticed that the bottom of her daughter's dress was unbuttoned.
The warrant alleges the toddler told her mother "the man did it," referring to the man who had been driving the car.
Martin allegedly had both hands on the child's torso when officers found him and was trying to duck down and hide between the seats, according to the warrant cited by the outlet.
The Atlanta Police Department's Special Victims Unit was brought into the investigation.
Martin allegedly told investigators he had been touching the child because he was trying to calm her down, according to 11Alive.
He also allegedly claimed he jumped into the vehicle because he was trying to "get back to New Jersey" and did not realize the toddler was in the backseat until after he drove away.

According to the arrest warrant, Martin also allegedly told investigators he realized there was an iPad inside the vehicle and discarded it because he believed it could be used to track him.
